documents.abstract: This qualitative case study explores how primary school educators in Cyprus integrate artificial intelligence (AI) into their teaching and professional practice within an education system at an early stage of AI adoption. Data were collected from fifteen educators through semi-structured interviews, concurrent think-aloud protocols, and AI-supported lesson plans. The data were analysed using an expanded Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), incorporating selected constructs from the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) and the AI-TPACK framework to examine individual, organisational, and contextual influences on AI adoption. Findings indicate that educators integrated AI into lesson planning, instructional differentiation, assessment design, multimedia development, and self-directed professional learning. Although participants demonstrated increasing confidence and professional agency in using AI, sustained implementation depended less on individual willingness than on the availability of organisational, pedagogical, and policy support. Limited infrastructure, fragmented professional development, ethical uncertainty, inconsistent leadership, and the absence of coherent institutional guidance constrained the transition from individual experimentation to systematic classroom integration. The study contributes to the growing literature on AI in primary education by demonstrating that meaningful AI implementation in early-adoption education systems is shaped by the interaction between teacher agency and institutional conditions rather than by technology acceptance alone. Based on these findings, a five-pillar framework is proposed to support responsible and sustainable AI integration through systemic governance, equitable access, embedded professional learning, curriculum and pedagogical alignment, and stakeholder engagement. While grounded in the Cypriot context, the findings offer insights that may inform AI implementation in comparable education systems.

documents.abstract: Purpose: This study examines key factors influencing the learning performance of Physical Education majors at a public vocational college in Henan Province and evaluates the effectiveness of a blended learning intervention. Research design, data and methodology: An Intervention Design and Implementation (IDI) framework with pre-IDI, IDI, and post-IDI stages was applied using mixed methods. Content validity and reliability were confirmed through expert review and a pilot test. Survey data from 80 students were analyzed using multiple linear regression. A 12-week blended learning intervention was then implemented with 40 students, followed by paired-sample t-tests and supportive interviews. Results: Regression analysis showed that behavioral engagement, cognitive engagement, learning motivation, active collaborative learning, and feedback significantly predicted learning performance, with feedback showing the strongest effect (β = 0.324). Paired-sample t-test results indicated significant improvements across all variables after the intervention, including learning performance (mean difference = 0.45). Interview findings aligned with the quantitative results, indicating higher engagement, motivation, collaboration, and more effective feedback use. Conclusions: The findings demonstrate that blended learning supported by structured pedagogy can significantly enhance learning performance in Physical Education. By embedding key learning principles into instructional design, this approach strengthens both learning processes and outcomes. The study provides empirical and theoretical insights for improving blended learning in vocational education contexts.

Learn how to identify who or what is interacting with your application using AgentCredia's Actor Classes Reference Card. This practical resource explains the four actor classifications: Human, Human + AI, Agent, and Unknown, along with the evidence used to support each classification. Understand the difference between verified, declared, inferred, and unknown evidence, why account authentication does not establish actor identity, and how to interpret AI agent activity without making unsupported assumptions. Ideal for SaaS platforms, API developers, security teams, and organizations preparing for AI-driven interactions.

Lightweight virtual reality (VR) can visually specify self-motion without body translation, but compact systems cannot readily reproduce body-scale forces. We tested whether ungrounded asymmetric vibration intended to evoke pulling changes maximum self-motion-speed ratings. Twenty-four adults completed a primary and a secondary within-participant experiment. In Experiment 1, optic flow at 10 or 15 m/s was presented alone, with symmetric vibration, or with asymmetric vibration whose perceived pull was velocity-aligned or velocity-opposed to visually specified self-motion. Both asymmetric mappings produced higher ratings than the visual-only and symmetric-vibration controls, whereas the mappings did not reliably differ. In Experiment 2, adding self-motion-specifying optic flow in the velocity-aligned configuration increased maximum-pulling-force ratings relative to haptic-only stimulation. A direct configuration-by-rating-type interaction showed that this effect was larger for pulling-force than vibration-intensity ratings obtained from the same trials. The tested pseudo-traction configurations thus changed reported self-motion magnitude, while Experiment 2 provided complementary rating-specificity evidence. Because asymmetric and symmetric stimulation also differed in waveform-dependent properties, the results are consistent with, but do not isolate, a contribution of the perceived pulling sensation. They do not establish a universal directional-mapping rule or a direct change in vection dynamics. For lightweight VR design, cue magnitude and force meaning are separable design decisions.

Despite growing generative artificial intelligence (GAI) adoption in language teaching, how teachers of languages other than English (LOTEs) navigate GAI integration remains understudied. The study combines grounded-theory analysis with fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) of 18 university LOTE teacher cases recruited through purposive and theoretical sampling. Grounded theory generated a model of factors influencing LOTE teachers’ engagement with GAI, and fsQCA identified four high-engagement configurations organized into two solution families. A supplementary qualitative account highlighted reservations concerning GAI’s pedagogical compatibility. The findings illustrate that GAI reproduces, rather than eliminates, the existing linguistic hierarchies in LOTE language education and theorize adaptive labor of LOTE teachers not just as a signal of high engagement but of deliberate, expertise-driven response to asymmetrical GAI tool design that privileges high-resource languages. This reframes GAI adoption as a linguistic equity issue with implications for differentiated professional development and equitable tool design.

European transport and logistics sectors are undergoing a transformative shift driven by the increasing adoption of data-driven solutions. This paper explores challenges and opportunities associated with implementing data-sharing frameworks and interoperable systems, drawing insights from European initiatives such as KEYSTONE and HOLOGISTICS projects and DTLF group. Fragmented data ecosystems and associated sociotechnical barriers, such as lack of inter-organisational trust and concerns over data sovereignty, significant barriers to realising the full potential of data-driven transport. However, innovations like federated platforms, real-time data utilisation and collaborative frameworks have demonstrated their ability to enhance operational efficiency, reduce environmental impact and improve resilience across multimodal transport networks. This paper presents valuable lessons learned, highlighting practical outcomes, including reduced times, optimised resource allocation, and emissions reductions. It also offers policy recommendations and a technological roadmap to address remaining barriers, scale solutions, and align with European Union’s strategic objectives for sustainability and digital integration, particularly in support of EU’s Green Deal and climate neutrality targets for 2050, also in line with the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development. By addressing these challenges and leveraging emerging technologies, Europe’s transport and logistics sectors can achieve cleaner, more resilient, and connected mobility systems, setting a global benchmark for sustainable innovation.

Smartphones are frequently used in stationary (i.e., static) contexts where users place them on surfaces for extended periods to support tasks such as following recipe instructions while cooking, accessing manuals while repairing, or practicing crafts like painting or pottery through video. However, interacting with a smartphone in these scenarios often requires direct touchscreen contact, which becomes problematic to execute easily when both of the user’s hands get wet, greasy, or contaminated with substances such as oils and chemicals. This is because it can cause liquid ingress or display staining when touching the smartphone, as well as the triggering of technical faults such as “ghost touches” or screen non-responsiveness due to the presence of wet or contaminated insulating material. Existing solutions face limitations: voice control struggles with environmental noise, while Back-of-Device interactions are inaccessible when the smartphone is placed on a surface. Accordingly, we introduce Unobtrusive Ferromagnetic Objects (UFO)—a lightweight, passive solution that enables touch-free interaction with smartphones using readily available ferromagnetic (FM) objects found in everyday settings in various forms, e.g., keys, spoons, screwdrivers, pens, and scales. UFO requires no modifications to the smartphone, object, environment, or surface, as it operates entirely through the built-in magnetometer. We conducted comprehensive technical and user-based (N=12) evaluations of the UFO technique across a wide range of real-world scenarios. The results demonstrated highly accurate identification of FM object-based inputs (98.9% on average) without requiring prior calibration, while maintaining consistent performance across diverse real world environments. Additionally, a user study (N = 21) demonstrated that the UFO approach achieved high task performance and low reported difficulty and fatigue when compared with direct touchscreen interaction under the matched temporal-gesture condition. These findings support the feasibility of UFO for providing touch-free input to smartphones placed on surfaces and motivate potential applications in situations where direct contact with the smartphone may be undesirable, including scenarios involving gloved or contaminated hands. By leveraging everyday objects as input tools, UFO presents an intuitive, scalable, and user-friendly alternative that complements traditional touchscreen interaction.

Bladder cancer is among the most recurrence-prone malignancies, and its management remains anchored to invasive cystoscopy and cytology, which have limited sensitivity. Urine, which is in direct contact with the tumor, carries a rich molecular cargo, including urinary tumor-derived DNA (utDNA), the tumor-derived fraction of urinary cell-free DNA, alongside methylation marks, extracellular vesicle (EV) cargo, and exfoliated cells. These components can now be interrogated through multi-omics profiling and interpreted using artificial intelligence (AI). In this Mini Review, we integrate these layers into a single translational framework: microfluidic “urine-on-chip” technologies convert a drop of urine into standardized, analysis-ready multi-omic data, while machine learning and deep learning models—increasingly governed by STARD-AI/TRIPOD + AI reporting standards—transform these data into diagnostic, prognostic, and treatment-response predictions. We highlight clinically mature anchors, including the utMeMA methylation assay (90.0%/83.1%), the Uromonitor mutation test (TERT/FGFR3/KRAS; 80.2%/96.9%, meta-analysis), chip-based cytometry for detecting high-grade disease, and an externally validated autonomous urine cytology system. These figures are assay-specific and should not be interpreted as platform-wide benchmarks. Finally, we define the priorities—pre-analytical standardization, external validation, and cost-effectiveness—that will advance urinary multi-omic AI from its current performance level into routine practice along a “detect–decide–treat–monitor” digital management pathway.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming criminal investigation and forensic science by enabling the rapid analysis of large volumes of digital and physical evidence. The integration of AI into criminal investigations enhances the efficiency of digital forensics, video and image analysis, biometric identification, DNA analysis, ballistic examination and cybercrime detection. Machine learning, computer vision and natural language processing assist investigators in identifying patterns, detecting anomalies, correlating evidence and reducing the time required for manual examination. Compared with traditional forensic methods, AI-driven systems offer greater scalability and automated evidence processing, although their accuracy and reliability depend on data quality, algorithmic design and expert validation. In India, provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (BNSS), particularly Sections 173, 176(3) and 185, provide a relevant procedural framework for electronic reporting, forensic crime-scene examination and the audio-video recording of searches. However, the adoption of AI in criminal investigations raises significant concerns regarding algorithmic bias, privacy, transparency, evidentiary reliability and legal admissibility. This study examines the major applications, benefits, limitations and legal implications of AI in criminal investigation, emphasising the importance of human oversight, scientific validation and procedural safeguards. It concludes that AI should function as an assistive investigative technology rather than a replacement for professional judgment and established forensic procedures.

Feedback is an important interaction channel in human–robot collaboration (HRC), yet feedback solicitation may affect users independently of whether their feedback changes robot behavior. This between-subjects study investigated how user-initiated and system-prompted feedback influence short-term trust development and perceived safety in a virtual industrial collaboration task. Forty-eight participants were assigned to either a system-prompted condition ( n = 23 ) , in which feedback was requested at predefined task milestones, or a user-initiated condition ( n = 25 ) , in which feedback could be provided at self-selected moments. Trust was assessed before and after the interaction, while perceived safety was measured afterward. A mixed ANCOVA revealed a significant time-by-condition interaction: trust increased in the system-prompted condition, compared to the user-initiated condition. Perceived safety did not differ between conditions. These findings suggest that feedback solicitation may function as an interaction-design feature that may shape short-term trust and feedback coverage under stable robot behavior.

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence has become an increasingly influential component of contemporary education, creating new opportunities for improving English language teaching methodology. AI-powered applications can support lesson planning, instructional material development, personalized learning, pronunciation practice, writing assessment, vocabulary acquisition, and the development of communicative competence. At the same time, their integration into educational practice raises important questions concerning pedagogical effectiveness, academic integrity, data privacy, teacher autonomy, and learners’ critical thinking. This article examines the methodological applications of artificial intelligence tools in English language teaching, focusing on their educational potential, practical implementation, and associated challenges. The study employs a qualitative, literature-based methodology drawing on research in educational technology, computer-assisted language learning, artificial intelligence, and English language pedagogy. The analysis identifies major areas in which AI can support teachers and learners, including lesson design, differentiated instruction, interactive communication, automated feedback, and formative assessment. It also examines the importance of teacher mediation, digital literacy, and responsible technology use.

Metro operators worldwide face critical fail-to-board events at centralised interchange stations, where local mitigation (e.g., schedule adjustments or empty-train insertion) can displace congestion downstream. We propose a calibrated digital twin of the Panama Metro integrated with two AI optimisation methods: a genetic algorithm and a deep reinforcement learning agent. Using real operational data from morning peak hours, the framework evaluates dispatching policies to minimise network-wide fail-to-board and is benchmarked against manual control and a commercial solver with station-level targets. The commercial solver reduced fail-to-board at Central Station by 37% but required 8–18 min per optimisation. The genetic algorithm achieved comparable reduction (33%) in 60–120 s while optimising network-wide performance. Deep reinforcement learning reached similar performance (32%) with $$\sim $$ ∼ 1 s inference, enabling near-real-time deployment in metro control rooms. Unlike station-level optimisation, network-wide optimisation prevents congestion displacement to upstream stations, resulting in lower spillover while maintaining similar fail-to-board reduction across the entire network.

Written intercultural communication is an essential competence for university students who study and work in linguistically and culturally diverse environments. Artificial intelligence (AI) tools can support this competence by providing timely language feedback, modelling alternative registers, helping learners consider audience expectations, and enabling iterative revision. However, fluent AI-generated text does not automatically develop intercultural understanding: systems may reproduce cultural stereotypes, overlook local context, or encourage overreliance. This article examines pedagogical ways of integrating AI into the teaching of written intercultural communication in higher education. Following an integrative, concept-oriented review of relevant scholarship, it proposes a classroom framework that combines AI-supported input, guided drafting, intercultural peer review, and human reflection. A practical matrix links learning objectives, AI-supported activities, and assessment criteria. The article argues that AI should function as a scaffold rather than an author, with transparent use, privacy protection, source checking, and student ownership built into course design. The proposed framework offers a practical basis for lesson planning and future empirical evaluation.

The expressive exploration of sonic spaces is a frequent mechanism of Digital Musical Instruments. These spaces can consist in sets of sounds, sonified data, interpolated synthesis presets and so on. Performers, whether novices or experts, might find it difficult to navigate such spaces due to their complexity and diversity. Extended Reality technologies enable the addition of visual elements over the physical space, providing visual feedback on the sonic space using colours, shapes or visual metaphors. However, it can be challenging to display the information without visual overload and while preserving the focus on musical gestures. In this article, we investigate different types of visualisations for the exploration of sonic spaces in Mixed Reality. We use drawing as an interaction metaphor, with strokes as a visual representation of a sonic trajectory. After evaluating various feedback options in a study with expert musical and visual artists, we conduct a controlled experiment with 18 novice users. The task was to reproduce sequences of sounds inside a sonic space by doing trajectories, while testing out different visualisation levels directly onto the strokes. The results did not reveal a statistically significant effect of the visualisations on the trajectories’ accuracy (with only anecdotal evidence for an absence of difference). However, participants preferred having higher levels of visualisation to guide them in their sonic exploration.

The rapid advancement of digital technologies particularly Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed educational practices worldwide, with artificial intelligence (AI) emerging as one of the most influential tools in reshaping teaching and learning; yet instructional delivery in many higher education science classrooms remains predominantly lecture-based. An investigative study on the awareness and utilization of artificial intelligence in the instructional delivery of Biology education at Akwa Ibom State University, Nigeria, was conducted using a descriptive survey research design. Three research questions and a hypothesis guided the study. The population of the study consisted of 923 students from level 200-400 in the entire program in the Department of Education, Akwa Ibom State University. A Sample of 234 students was selected using Taro Yamane’s formula. Awareness of Artificial Intelligence Questionnaire (AAIQ) and Utilization of Artificial Intelligence Questionnaire (UAIQ) was developed, with a reliability coefficient will be determined using Cronbach's alpha. Hard copy of the questionnaires will be administered to respondents. Frequency counts, mean, standard deviation, and one-way ANOVA were used to analyze the data obtained. Results showed that a significant difference existed in the level of awareness of Artificial Intelligence among Biology Education students across the different academic levels; result also indicate that a statistically significant difference existed in the level of utilization of Artificial Intelligence among Biology Education students across the different academic levels, and male students used Artificial Intelligence more compared to their female counterparts. Based on the findings, it was recommended, among others, that tertiary institutions and governments should integrate the utilization of Artificial Intelligence among students in other to have appropriate knowledge and skills to meet with increasing globalization and needs of society.

documents.abstract: Despite continued advances in smart glasses’ display capabilities, on-device touch input remains fundamentally constrained by the thin temple form factor and its narrow, primarily horizontal input space. In this work, we present VertiTouch, a novel system that vertically expands the touch input space of thin temples of smart glasses, directly enabling self-contained dexterous 2D touch interaction. Rather than restricting contact to the fingertip, VertiTouch leverages the entire finger to extend the 6 mm vertical input axis to the length of the finger. We implemented a system prototype through iterative refinements and evaluated it in two controlled studies with 12 participants using a Fitts’ law-style 2D target selection task spanning 36.2° × 36.2° visual angle. With high-precision external tracking, VertiTouch performed within approximately 10% of a physically large 70 × 50 mm temple touchpad representing an upper-bound reference for on-device touch area, both in mean target selection time and throughput estimate. Using only compact on-device sensors, the standalone prototype achieved a mean selection time of 2.4 s on the same task. Overall, our findings demonstrate that self-contained rich 2D touch input is possible on smart glasses alone by virtually extending the vertical input space along the index finger.

Virus-host association prediction is fundamental to virus-related disease control and phage therapy, yet many existing tools require candidate-host genome sequences, which may be unavailable for some eukaryotic hosts or impractical to search at the scale of large virome studies. We present VHSeek, a supervised virus-host association predictor that integrates DNA- and protein-derived viral representations. VHSeek combines nucleotide representations from AIDO.DNA and protein representations from ESM2 to learn virus-host association patterns, and then transfers predictions through known host taxonomies from lower to higher ranks. During inference, VHSeek uses viral sequence data and known host taxonomies, without host sequence data. Compared with iPHoP, the state-of-the-art baseline evaluated in this study, VHSeek improves genus-level maximum F1 score (Fmax), Top-1 accuracy, and area under the precision–recall curve (AUPR) by 12%, 19%, and 27%, respectively. Confidence thresholding enables abstention and reduces false discoveries. On the processed IMG/VR v4.1 metagenomic collection, VHSeek expands effective host coverage from 36.5% to 64.5% using a validation-calibrated confidence threshold. VHSeek prioritizes candidate viruses and reservoir hosts with potential human health impacts, including multi-host hypotheses in which one virus may be associated with humans and additional hosts (e.g., Saboya virus with Homo sapiens and Culicidae) not currently captured in the dataset.

Violence and harassment in the world of work have increasingly been recognised as structural violations of labour rights, human dignity, and occupational health and safety. In response to these challenges, the International Labour Organization adopted Convention No. 190, establishing for the first time a comprehensive international standard on the elimination of violence and harassment at work. Albania ratified Convention No. 190 in 2022, thereby assuming the obligation to align its domestic legal and institutional framework with the Convention’s requirements. However, the transition from formal ratification to effective implementation remains complex and not automatic. Moreover, Albanian labour law is not yet equipped to give effect to the Convention's innovative concept of the “world of work,” as non-standard and emerging forms of employment remain largely unaccounted for in the existing domestic legal framework. This article examines the extent to which the Albanian legal and institutional framework complies with the standards set by ILO Convention No. 190 and identifies the main gaps hindering its effective application. Methodologically, the article combines normative legal analysis with descriptive findings from an online survey of 153 employed law students at the Faculty of Law, University of Tirana. The survey examined respondents’ awareness of workplace harassment and Convention No. 190, their knowledge of reporting mechanisms, and perceived barriers to reporting. The findings reveal a fragmented system of legal protection, characterised by the absence of a unified definition of workplace harassment, unclear institutional responsibilities, and weak enforcement mechanisms. Within the surveyed group, the findings indicate limited awareness of available remedies and uncertainty about reporting mechanisms. The article argues that without addressing these normative, institutional, and cultural shortcomings, the protective potential of Convention No. 190 risks remaining largely symbolic. The paper concludes by proposing targeted legal and policy recommendations to strengthen enforcement mechanisms, improve institutional coordination, and enhance awareness and reporting practices in the Albanian context. Digital learning technologies offer expanding opportunities for higher education, yet little is known about how immersive virtual reality (VR), traditional 2D video, and emerging artificial intelligence (AI)-generated podcasts compare in content-equivalent settings. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, the Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning, and Self-Efficacy Theory, this study examined effects of medium on short-term knowledge acquisition, motivation, perceived agency, and self-efficacy. German university students were randomly assigned to VR, 2D video, or an AI-generated podcast and engaged with equivalent content on the history of the German National Theatre in Weimar for approximately 6 min. A pre-post design assessed changes across outcomes. The medium produced no significant differences in knowledge acquisition or self-efficacy, and most directional expectations were unsupported. A small effect emerged for a composite affective measure (partial η2 = 0.072), favoring VR over 2D video, while VR and the AI-generated podcast did not differ significantly. As no formal equivalence test was conducted, non-significant differences should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalence. The findings provide preliminary evidence that AI-generated podcasts may represent a low-cost, scalable option for higher education, although conclusions are limited to one short intervention, one topic, one AI platform, and immediate post-exposure outcomes. Further research should examine broader contexts.

In 3D environments, factors such as hand and tracker jitter can substantially degrade user performance during ray-casting selection. This makes it difficult for users to complete selection tasks involving target objects with small visible areas, since small targets require higher levels of precision. This paper proposes VoroCast —a Voronoi-based two-stage selection technique designed for dense environments in VR, aimed at reducing the precision required for the task. In the first stage, VoroCast captures candidate objects via cone casting; then it dynamically generates a semi-transparent disambiguation disc based on Voronoi partitioning. VoroCast , based on Voronoi partitioning, mathematically guarantees a nearest-neighbor-based selection area for each candidate object’s selection area, which enlarges the effective target width relevant to Fitts’ Law and thereby reduces pointing difficulty. To evaluate the performance of VoroCast , we recruited participants to compare it against two state-of-the-art techniques in dense virtual scenes. The results demonstrate that VoroCast achieves significant advantages in selection efficiency, accuracy, and user preference.

Virtual sensing can reduce the cost of generating sensor datasets for human activity recognition and ubiquitous sensing, yet users must still translate sensing intent into concrete scene configurations. This fragmentation makes it difficult to translate sensing goals into concrete configurations and refine them as results emerge. We present VsensAgent , a human–agent interface that grounds an LLM-powered agent in a shared 3D simulation environment. Users combine natural-language delegation with direct scene manipulation, while the agent can inspect scene state, configure sensors and avatar motions, record data, and support signal analysis. We conducted a task-based study of VsensAgent in which 12 participants completed 36 virtual sensing authoring sessions. Analysis of interaction logs, authored configurations, and post-task interviews showed that participants progressively developed intent through executable scene states, shifted control between agent delegation and direct manipulation at the level of individual operations, and treated agent proposals as editable starting points. These findings frame virtual sensor generation as progressive, collaborative authoring and inform the design of agents for stateful workflows.

Building advanced software and AI solutions requires more than technical expertise. Many projects perform well during testing but face challenges when integrated into real business environments. Complex workflows, existing infrastructure, and changing requirements can make implementation difficult. This is where a forward deployed engineer helps connect technology with practical business needs. What Is a Forward Deployed Engineer? An FDE engineer is a technical specialist who works directly with customers to understand their challenges, develop tailored solutions, and support implementation. Unlike traditional software engineers who primarily focus on product development, FDEs combine hands-on engineering with close collaboration with business teams. Their responsibilities often include system integration, troubleshooting, customization, and ensuring that technical solutions align with operational requirements. Understanding the Forward Deployed Engineer Role The forward deployed engineer role goes beyond writing code. These specialists help organizations translate business requirements into working technical solutions, especially when projects involve complex integrations or rapidly changing needs. Key responsibilities include: – Understanding customer workflows and technical challenges – Integrating software with existing business systems – Customizing solutions for specific operational needs – Resolving implementation issues – Supporting deployment and continuous improvement This approach helps businesses reduce the gap between development and real-world adoption. The Importance of AI Forward Deployed Engineers As organizations introduce artificial intelligence into their operations, the demand for specialists who understand both AI technology and business processes continues to grow. An AI forward deployed engineer helps companies move beyond prototypes by connecting AI models with enterprise applications, internal databases, and existing workflows. These specialists also address technical limitations, improve system reliability, and ensure that AI solutions work effectively in production environments. Their involvement can be particularly valuable for businesses implementing AI assistants, workflow automation, and enterprise AI integrations. Conclusion Forward deployed engineering provides a practical approach to implementing complex technologies in real business environments. By combining technical expertise with direct customer collaboration, FDEs help organizations overcome integration challenges, adapt solutions to operational needs, and achieve more reliable results. As AI adoption expands, forward deployed engineers are becoming increasingly important for companies looking to turn promising technologies into scalable business solutions.

documents.abstract: LLM-based agents are now capable of deleting personal data on users’ behalf, yet what they need to reason about has not been studied. We report preliminary findings from 15 semi-structured interviews on how people specify deletion intent across different digital domains. We treat filter-based interfaces as a diagnostic. Their failure modes reveal the reasoning LLM agents would need instead. First, we empirically map the semantic reasoning requirements for LLM-based deletion agents. Most participants described criteria grounded in relational context, imagined audience, and personal history that no filter can represent. Second, we observe a trust paradox. Users with the most semantically complex needs were least willing to delegate, due to privacy concerns. Third, we find that describing what to delete clearly enough for an agent is itself a form of disclosure. These are initial findings; we are now investigating what they mean for how LLM-based deletion agents should be designed.

The growing use of generative AI (GenAI) in higher education raises concerns about students’ cognitive atrophy, as many students are tempted to delegate tasks that require deep reasoning to GenAI. This study examines university students’ perceptions of Minimalist, a dialogic AI assistant designed to scaffold a discourse synthesis task through a specific discourse architecture, and asks them to engage in critical thinking while doing the task, rather than generating content for them. Twenty-three university students interacted with Minimalist during a single-session discourse synthesis task, after which they completed an open-ended questionnaire. Inductive thematic analysis revealed six themes. Findings demonstrate that dialogic scaffolding was experienced as pedagogically valuable and yielded three design principles, the Dialogic Scaffolding Principle, the Dialogic Threshold, and the Automation-Cognition Balance Problem, with implications for the future design of educational AI systems.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) challenges traditional boundaries of academic authorship, potentially weakening students’ psychological ownership and accountability. This three-wave longitudinal study examined prospective associations among human–AI co-authorship ambiguity (HAAA), psychological ownership, responsibility dilution, and self-reported GenAI-related academic behaviors. Data from 586 Chinese high school students (91.3% retention) were analyzed using a random-intercept cross-lagged panel model to distinguish within-person fluctuations from stable between-person differences. Across both intervals, greater HAAA predicted lower psychological ownership ( β = −0.283 and −0.265) and greater responsibility dilution ( β = 0.251 and 0.230). Lower psychological ownership predicted greater responsibility dilution ( β = −0.291 and −0.275), which subsequently predicted more frequent GenAI-related academic behaviors ( β = 0.332 and 0.347; all p < 0.001). Significant two-lag indirect associations linked HAAA to later academic-behavior scores through psychological ownership ( b = 0.045) and responsibility dilution ( b = 0.077). These findings highlight the importance of authorship clarity, psychological ownership, and personal accountability in GenAI-assisted learning. Although causal conclusions are unwarranted, the results suggest that academic-integrity education should emphasize students’ intellectual contributions and responsibility for AI-assisted work.

documents.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can suggest wording, explain language, and increasingly contribute to feedback and assessment. The central issue is not only what these systems generate, but when learners, teachers, and institutions begin to treat their outputs as reasons for judging language. Existing research addresses language ideology, distributed agency, algorithmic normativity, trust, assessment, and AI governance, but these literatures use different concepts for influence, authority, and institutional power. This article develops a multilevel framework of linguistic authority escalation through a critical integrative review focused primarily on English-dominant higher-education writing and assessment. In the framework, authority in the strict sense refers to attributed epistemic or normative standing; operational uptake is causal influence, and regulatory consequentiality is institutional power. The framework differentiates the initiator, subject, decision-maker, and accountable actor, and represents the source of authorisation, the subject’s degree of meaningful choice, and the durability of system embedding as co-occurring configurational conditions rather than alternative routes. It also distinguishes epistemic warrant, procedural legitimacy, substantive linguistic justice, and assessment validity as different standards for evaluating AI-mediated judgement. A literature-grounded worked case shows how the same model suggestion can remain optional assistance or acquire institutional force depending on these relations. The framework helps educational linguists identify when GenAI support preserves evaluative control and when opaque linguistic norms become difficult to contest, directing pedagogy and governance towards norm-explicit feedback, meaningful alternatives, task-specific evidence, appeal, and clear answerability.

Artificial intelligence safety research compares systems' answers and actions with output probabilities, generated reasoning, internal activations and monitoring judgments. These measurements can disagree about what a system knows, what influenced its response and whether unwanted behavior occurred. This critical tutorial review organizes the emerging literature around five comparisons: relative sensitivity, incremental value, functional dissociation, causal intervention and targeted robustness. Worked examples distinguish reported findings, their inferential limits and informative follow-up comparisons. The comparisons are introduced through simpler settings and then applied where models respond to evaluation, withhold capabilities or make other evidence less revealing. Three conclusions connect research on knowledge elicitation, reasoning faithfulness, evaluation awareness, deliberate underperformance and monitoring. Measurements that agree under one condition need not remain interchangeable under another. Failure to recover information does not by itself establish its removal. And a measurement's usefulness belongs to the complete procedure and the conditions of use, including opportunities to influence the evidence. Human research on perception, memory, verbal reports and concealed information supplies methodological resources without any assumption of shared mechanisms. Three concrete extensions of existing experiments illustrate controlled relearning after unlearning, the information a reasoning report adds beyond an observer, and adaptation against individual monitors and their combination. An experiment-level source guide supports the synthesis. The aim is to make dissociations useful for cumulative safety research: not merely as differences between scores, but as evidence that changes an interpretation or determines the next informative experiment.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Regret follows from a person’s own choice; disappointment from circumstances outside their control. We benchmark large language model (LLM) configurations on separating the two in 2019 low-rated Amazon product reviews. Two independent human annotators labeled 385 reviews (Cohen’s κ=0.80): 200 drawn at random and 185 drawn where systems label regret. Unweighted scores describe this enriched set; stratum weights give pool estimates. We compare GPT-4o with and without theory-based definitions and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) across the regret literature, an adapted Speculative RAG pipeline, our original pipeline, a regret-cue lexicon, and a supervised TF-IDF classifier, which rarely detected regret (F1 = 0.12). On the 372 reviews with an agreed label, GPT-4o without retrieval agreed best with the annotators (κ=0.73 with label names, 0.72 with definitions; F1 for regret 0.75, or 0.73 weighted to the pool). Adding retrieval to the definitions lowered agreement to κ=0.45 (McNemar p=1.9×10−8), mainly by labeling product complaints as regret. Speculative RAG with a GPT-4o-mini drafter (κ=0.20) and the original pipeline (κ=0.16) did worst. Asked to choose between the two emotions, the annotators placed 2.0% of random reviews on the regret side; the LLM systems’ estimates on the same reviews ranged from 1.5% to 21.5%. For this distinction, a plain GPT-4o prompt was more accurate than retrieving the regret literature and used under a quarter of the input tokens.

Artificial intelligence is entering psychotherapy at almost every point of clinical work: therapist training, screening and detection, risk prediction, diagnostic support and treatment planning, patient education, chatbot-delivered session content, between-session tracking, supervision, and documentation. Discussion of the associated dangers to this process has so far been overwhelmingly patient directed. This narrative review addresses these questions from a futures-oriented perspective: what AI may do to psychotherapists as professionals. We first map current and emerging applications across the phases of therapy. We then distinguish four forms of competence loss reported in the wider clinical literature, namely deskilling, never-skilling, mis-skilling, and moral deskilling, and use them to structure a function-by-function analysis of nine clinical tasks. The risks we identify, most of which rest on extrapolation from medicine and education and are therefore best read as hypotheses, extend beyond technical skill. Algorithmic flags may redistribute clinical attention, and accountability may shift from the quality of judgement to adherence to procedure. Case formulation may close prematurely, and theoretical pluralism may narrow toward the traditions best represented in training data. Findings that chatbots are rated as more empathic than clinicians may threaten professional identity, while supervision may lose its relational and formative functions. We then set out four possible trajectories for the field: AI as a support to professional judgement, gradual dependency, standardized AI-mediated practice, and systems designed explicitly to preserve and cultivate expertise, together with the drivers that may lead toward each. Implications are drawn for training, clinical governance, and professional ethics.

documents.abstract: Selective prediction systems improve the safety of clinical artificial intelligence by deferring ambiguous cases to human experts while automating high-confidence decisions. However, this safety mechanism relies entirely on the premise that uncertainty scores accurately reflect clinical ambiguity. In prognostic tasks characterized by severe class imbalance, where the clinical outcome of interest is a minority, this assumption breaks down. Standard uncertainty measures cease to capture clinically aligned ambiguity; instead, they become a proxy for class membership, systematically penalizing minority patients regardless of their individual predictive clarity. We characterize three structural failure modes driving this breakdown: the mismatch between standard entropy’s mathematical peak and the clinical decision threshold; the asymmetric spatial penalty in margin-based uncertainty; and structural uncertainty divergence of minority predictions driven by data scarcity. We propose three counter-mechanisms: an empirically validated threshold-aware ambiguity score that realigns maximum uncertainty with the clinical threshold, a class-conditioned rejection (CCR) mechanism ranking patients within their predicted trajectory rather than globally, and a class-stratified evaluation metric that prevents global risk scores from concealing automated minority exclusion. Across 56 synthetic conditions and three neurodegenerative cohorts spanning severe class imbalance to near-balanced conditions (multiple sclerosis, Parkinson’s Disease, Alzheimer’s Disease), our framework consistently maintained bounded, balanced risk across trajectories. In contrast, global metrics either collapsed minority Sensitivity or protected the minority at the expense of majority patients. An ablation study confirmed that applying CCR with standard entropy fails to protect the minority because it breaks within-class monotonicity when \(\tau \neq 0.5\) . Combining CCR with threshold-aware metrics restores strict monotonicity, correctly identifies ambiguous patients, and safely mitigates minority exclusion. Under clinical class imbalance, standard uncertainty quantification measures dataset sparsity rather than clinical ambiguity, creating a systemic illusion of safety. This bias is a correctable structural flaw. Clinical pipelines deploying selective prediction under imbalance should adopt threshold-aligned uncertainty measures and class-stratified evaluation. This reduces class-specific risk imbalance, supporting safer selective prediction under the evaluated conditions without silently excluding the most vulnerable patients.

documents.abstract: As large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into smart home assistants (SHAs), voice interactions are moving beyond constrained commands toward open-ended conversations, increasing ambiguity in user requests. Therefore, this study investigates how request ambiguity and response explainability affect users’ perceived trust, satisfaction, and pleasure in the context of LLM-based smart home assistant (SHA). A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 211 participants across three scenarios: device control, information inquiry, and schedule planning. Results showed that request ambiguity negatively affected all three outcomes under low explainability. LLM response explainability substantially improved users’ evaluations of trust, satisfaction, and pleasure under high ambiguity, mitigating the negative effects by clarifying how the assistant interpreted user intent and why it generated a particular response. These findings advance understanding of ambiguity and explainability in human–AI interaction from a user experience perspective and highlight the importance of adaptive explanation strategies in LLM-based SHAs.

Background. Women’s working conditions, including pay, contractual security, occupational health, working time, harassment, and the interface between paid work and care, are central to decent work and gender equality agendas; however, scholarship addressing them is spread across development studies, sociology, economics, occupational health, and ergonomics. To the best of our knowledge, no systematic map exists in this field. Methods. Methods: We conducted a bibliometric analysis of 614 Scopus-indexed journal articles and book chapters on women workers and working conditions published between 2000 and 2025. Performance analysis (production, citations, h- and g-indices, and collaboration) and science mapping (keyword co-occurrence, thematic mapping, trend topics, and reference-year analysis) were carried out using Biblioshiny and VOSviewer. Results. Output grew at approximately 9% per year, and half of all documents (49.5%) appeared between 2020 and 2025. The literature is dispersed: 398 sources carried 614 documents, 77.1% of sources contributed a single document, and 95.3% of the 1,363 authors appeared only once. Gender, Work and Organisation , Social Science and Medicine , and International Journal of Industrial Ergonomics were the most productive sources. The United Kingdom (57 documents with a corresponding author), the USA (51), and India (48) led production, but India’s average citation count (6.1) was far below that of the United Kingdom (31.1) and Australia (29.1), partly because more than half of India’s affiliation count was added after 2022. International co-authorship was limited (19.8% of documents with identified corresponding authors). Keyword mapping revealed five clusters: labour markets and informal work; work-family balance and inequality in Europe; occupational health and ergonomics; psychosocial well-being and harassment; and socioeconomic context, with “working conditions” as the bridging concept. Trend topics moved from ergonomics and musculoskeletal disorders to gender discrimination, inequality, mental health, decent work, and COVID-19. Conclusions. The field is expanding rapidly but remains fragmented, geographically uneven, and weakly connected across its social science and health streams. Priorities include research on informal and platform work in the Global South, comparative and collaborative designs, and integrated frameworks that link structural, organisational and health perspectives.

As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes embedded in organizational work, understanding its implications for employees’ proactive career self-management is increasingly important. Drawing on the social cognitive model of career self-management, this study examines whether employee-AI collaboration is associated with career engagement through thriving at work and whether perceived human control influences these relationships. Three-wave survey data were collected at 2-week intervals from 255 employees using AI-enabled systems at work in China. Results showed that employee–AI collaboration was positively associated with thriving at work, which, in turn, was positively associated with career engagement. Perceived human control strengthened the positive relationship between employee–AI collaboration and thriving, suggesting that employees who perceived greater ability to influence AI interactions experienced greater developmental benefits from collaboration. Theoretical contributions and practical implications are discussed.

The integration of generative artificial intelligence technologies into design processes accelerates prototyping speed in the development of mobile user interfaces and enables the automated generation of visual components. However, the rapid and aesthetically consistent production of digital interfaces does not necessarily imply that these interfaces meet the requirements of diverse user groups. Particularly in designs supporting the independent access of individuals with orthopedic disabilities and fine motor skill impairments to digital services, it is crucial to consider physical interaction requirements and accessibility metrics. The underrepresentation of individuals with disabilities in the training datasets of generative AI systems brings about the risk that the needs of these users fail to be reflected in automatically generated designs. Accordingly, this study aims to comparatively examine the mobile interfaces generated by Visily AI, Figma AI, and Rocket AI platforms to support urban service access for individuals with orthopedic disabilities, thereby revealing the strengths and limitations of these tools in terms of accessible design. The theoretical framework of the study is established on digital accessibility, universal design principles, Gestalt perceptual theory, and WCAG 2.2. Digital accessibility ensures users with diverse requirements can access digital services independently. Universal design forms the foundation of inclusive design through principles like equitable use and low physical effort, mitigating touch screen difficulties. Gestalt perceptual theory allows evaluating visual organization and hierarchy through figure-ground relationships, proximity, similarity, and continuity. Meanwhile, WCAG 2.2 criteria examine contrast and touch-target dimensions. Addressing these theoretical approaches collectively enables evaluating interfaces regarding aesthetic qualities, usability, and motor accessibility. The research was designed as a comparative case study within the qualitative research approach. The review material consists of interfaces generated by Visily AI, Figma AI, and Rocket AI based on the "FreeMov" mobile application scenario structured to support urban mobility and independent living for individuals with orthopedic disabilities. To ensure comparability, a standardized prompt set containing expectations regarding the target user profile, screen hierarchy, functional requirements, and touch areas was employed. A total of 32 unique screenshots covering accessible route planning, community feeds, venue filters, event calendars, user profiles, and emergency functions (5 from Visily, 7 from Figma, 11 from Rocket) were archived without subsequent iteration. Data were analyzed using the Mobile Interface Accessibility and Design Review Framework through document and descriptive analysis techniques, with independent expert evaluations ensuring qualitative rigor in terms of visual hierarchy, usability, WCAG compliance, universal design, and Gestalt organization. The research findings demonstrate that the three platforms exhibit distinct design tendencies regarding interface architecture, information layout, and assistive functions. Visily AI stood out with its card-based modular structure, typographic hierarchy, and vertical continuity, supporting scannability and visual integrity through grouped contents and color-emphasized primary actions. However, the dense clustering of secondary informational labels, weakened information differentiation in map screens, positioning of micro-interaction components in narrow areas, and poor contrast of light-toned labels on light backgrounds posed limitations in terms of usability and accessibility. In the interfaces generated by Figma AI, the balanced use of negative space, component balance, and wide action buttons drew attention, providing targeting convenience for users with limited motor control. A minimalist bottom navigation structure and flexible calendar, list, and map event views supported diverse navigation preferences. In contrast, significant limitations included insufficient differentiation of map markers, close positioning of search and filter components, missing clear close controls on info cards, narrow touch areas for secondary icons, and low contrast of light gray texts on light backgrounds. Rocket AI distinguished itself through voice search support, accessibility status codes, filtering options, and direct emergency communication functions. Bottom sheets opening on the map to preserve context, filter resetting controls, and wide primary action buttons supported user control and interaction ease. Alternative interaction options like voice search reduced physical interaction requirements. Nonetheless, overlapping geographical details caused visual clutter, secondary texts and passive indicators exhibited insufficient contrast, search components in upper regions hindered single-handed reach, small close icons, and language mixing posed design inconsistencies. The comparative evaluation among platforms revealed that while each tool offers advantages in certain design dimensions, none of them fully and spontaneously meet accessibility requirements. Visily AI stood out in information grouping and page layout integrity, Figma AI in negative space usage and wide primary interaction areas, and Rocket AI in assistive component variety. Common issues across all platforms included insufficient contrast in small texts, close placement of secondary icons, and visual density in map screens. These findings demonstrate that contemporary aesthetic orderliness is insufficient regarding physical accessibility and motor ergonomics, highlighting the need to address accessibility alongside technical standards and user requirements. The results indicate that generative AI should be evaluated as an early-stage co-creator rather than an independent solution replacing the designer. It is recommended to explicitly incorporate WCAG 2.2 contrast, touch target requirements, and thumb-reach expectations into design prompts. Generated interfaces must undergo evaluation via contrast analysis tools, screen reader simulators, and touch area controls before implementation, with manual reorganization under human supervision. Limitations include static screenshot analysis, exclusion of underlying code structures, and lack of direct interactive testing with orthopedic disabled users. Future studies should conduct task completion tests with motor-impaired cohorts and examine interactive prototypes. Ultimately, the study emphasizes the importance of combining automated production with expert human supervision in inclusive design processes.

documents.abstract: The rapid development of research in the field of artificial intelligence underscores the need for a systematic organization of knowledge regarding its relationship with economic growth and development. This study aims to describe the publication dynamics, geographical distribution, thematic structure, and temporal characteristics of academic work in this field. The scope of the research encompasses international publications focused on artificial intelligence, economic growth, development, and productivity. The empirical basis consists of 3,192 English-language articles and reviews indexed in the Scopus database between 1987 and 2025. Using VOSviewer software, a bibliometric analysis and thematic mapping were conducted based on the co-occurrence of author-provided keywords. By segmenting the keywords - using a threshold of 10 occurrences - a network of 133 keywords was created, and organized into 8 thematic clusters. The research findings indicate that publication activity was concentrated primarily toward the end of the period under study, with 71.6% of the articles in the sample published in period between 2023 and 2025. The most prominent research originated from China, the United States, India, and the United Kingdom. The topics addressed in the research include areas such as productivity and innovation, digitalization and "green" transformation, forecasting, decision support, and applied analytics. Publications on subjects such as generative artificial intelligence, explainable machine learning, inclusive finance, and the energy transition have emerged relatively recently. This study contributes to the field by analyzing the research landscape and distinguishing between artificial intelligence as a driver of economic change and as a tool for analyzing processes of change. The study concludes that while the rise in publication activity reflects growing academic interest, this does not, in itself, demonstrate a positive impact of artificial intelligence on overall economic growth.These findings help refine future research directions and highlight the limitations of using bibliometric indicators to guide economic policy. Key words: artificial intelligence, economic growth, economic development, productivity, bibliometric analysis, thematic mapping, machine learning.

The aim of this article is to assess how generative artificial intelligence use relates to perceived changes in personal productivity and verification workload in hybrid teams in Kazakhstan. The study adopted an exploratory cross-sectional design. Data were collected in August–September 2026 through an online survey administered via Google Forms. Employees of Kazakhstan-registered IT companies and organizational digitalization departments were recruited through convenience and snowball sampling. Of the 100 responses received, 93 met the hybrid work criterion. Analyses directly related to AI use were based on responses from 86 users. The analysis included descriptive statistics, assessment of the internal consistency of measurement blocks, and item-level Spearman correlations. Holm correction was applied to multiple comparisons. Increased personal productivity was reported by 66.3% of users, while 61.6% reported high AI verification workload. High verification workload was common across all productivity groups, including 34 of the 57 respondents reporting productivity gains (59.6%). AI use frequency was positively associated with the direction of perceived productivity change (ρ = 0.338) and verification workload (ρ = 0.409). Associations between general digital workload and team outcomes did not reach statistical significance after Holm correction. The findings suggest that the perceived benefits of AI use can coexist with additional effort devoted to verifying its outputs. Unlike task-level experiments, the study measures perceived AI benefits and the effort of verifying AI outputs within the same survey and treats verification workload separately from general digital workload. To the authors’ knowledge, such evidence has not previously been reported for hybrid teams in Kazakhstan. The analysis distinguished general digital workload, the demands of learning new tools, and AI verification workload. The study’s practical contribution is to highlight the need to account for verification, revision, and coordination costs alongside initial output preparation when assessing AI effectiveness. The conclusions are based on self-reported assessments and do not establish causal relationships. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence, hybrid teams, perceived productivity, digital workload, verification workload, AI governance.

В условиях цифровой трансформации экономики актуализируется потребность в специалистах, обладающих современными профессиональными компетенциями в области программной инженерии. В статье представлна авторская педагогическая модель формирования профессиональной компетентности бакалавров программной инженерии, основанная на интеграции международной концепции CDIO (Conceive, Design, Implement, Operate) с традиционными подходами российского инженерного образования. Разработанная модель включает шесть взаимосвязанных блоков: целевой (определяет цели и задачи в контексте требований ФГОС ВО 3++, профессиональных стандартов и запросов работодателей), методологический (базируется на синтезе компетентностного, системного, деятельностного и личностно-ориентированного подходов), структурно-содержательный (операционализирует компетенции ПК-1 и ПК-2 через модульную организацию дисциплины), организационный (определяет методы, формы и средства обучения от объяснительно-иллюстративных до исследовательских), технологический (устанавливает семиэтапную последовательность реализации от диагностики до коррекции), критериально-оценочный (обеспечивает трехкомпонентную оценку мотивационного, когнитивного и деятельностного аспектов компетентности). Экспериментальная апробация модели проводилась в течение трех лет на базе Чувашского государственного университета с участием студентов направления «Программная инженерия». Эффективность модели оценивалась путем сопоставления достигнутых результатов с эталонными показателями, разработанными экспертным сообществом из числа ведущих специалистов-практиков IT-индустрии на основе анализа профессиональных стандартов и квалификационных требований работодателей. Результаты показали статистически значимый рост уровня сформированности профессиональной компетентности: средний балл вырос с 3,5 до 7,8 (из 10 возможных), что составляет 78 % приближения к эталонному уровню. Качественный анализ выявил повышение самостоятельности студентов в решении нестандартных задач, развитие навыков командной работы и проектного управления, рост внутренней мотивации к профессиональной деятельности. Практическая значимость исследования заключается в возможности адаптации модели для модернизации образовательных программ подготовки IT-специалистов, а также в разработке инструментария объективной оценки качества профессиональной подготовки выпускников. The digital transformation of the economy has intensified the demand for software engineering professionals with up-to-date professional competencies. This article presents an original pedagogical model for developing the professional competence of bachelor’s students in software engineering, integrating the international CDIO framework (Conceive, Design, Implement, Operate) with traditional approaches to Russian engineering education. The developed model comprises six interrelated components: target block (defines goals and tasks within the framework of the Federal State Educational Standards (FSES) of Higher Education 3++ and professional standards); methodological block (based on a synthesis of competence-based, systemic, activity-based, and learner-centered approaches); structural-content block (operationalizes the Professional Competence-1 and Professional Competence-2 through modular discipline organization); organizational block (determines teaching methods, forms, and tools – from expository-illustrative to research-based approaches); technological block (establishes a seven-stage implementation sequence from diagnosis to corrective actions); criterion-based assessment block (provides a three-dimensional evaluation of motivational, cognitive, and behavioral aspects of competence). The experimental validation of the model was conducted over three years at Chuvash State University with participation from students majoring in “Software Engineering”. The effectiveness of the model was assessed by comparing achieved outcomes against benchmark indicators established by an expert community of leading IT industry practitioners, based on analysis of professional standards and employer qualification requirements. Results demonstrated a statistically significant improvement in the level of professional competence: the average score increased from 3.5 to 7.8 (on a scale of 10), representing a 78% approach toward the benchmark level. Qualitative analysis revealed enhanced student independence in solving non-standard problems, improved teamwork and project management skills, and increased intrinsic motivation toward professional activities. The practical implication of this study lies in the model’s adaptability for modernizing educational programs preparing IT specialists, as well as in the development of objective assessment tools for evaluating the quality of graduate professional training.

الملخص:تهدف هذه الدراسة الاستكشافية إلى تحليل كيفية انتقال جامعة الجيل الرابع من الدور التقليدي المتمثل في إنتاج المعرفة إلى توظيف مخرجات البحث العلمي والتكنولوجيا في إنشاء الشركات الناشئة وتحقيق قيمة مضافة للمجتمع، مع التركيز بصورة خاصة على الذكاء الاصطناعي. واعتمدت الدراسة الجامعة التقنية الدنماركية (DTU) حالةً دراسية، باستخدام منهج وصفي تحليلي قائم على الاستقراء الوثائقي وتحليل محتوى التقارير السنوية لـDTU وDTU Skylab، والصفحات الرسمية والبرامج والأدلة المنشورة ذات الصلة بالشركات الناشئة والتمويل والنمذجة الأولية ونقل التكنولوجيا والذكاء الاصطناعي. أظهرت النتائج أن DTU دعم 399 فريقًا من فرق الشركات الناشئة خلال عام 2024، في حين أسهم طلبة وموظفو الجامعة في تأسيس 120 شركة ناشئة جديدة، كما ارتفعت الاستثمارات في شركات DTU الناشئة من 0.7 مليار كرونة دنماركية سنة 2020 إلى 2.6 مليار كرونة سنة 2024.وتبين الدراسة أن نجاح إنشاء الشركات الناشئة يرتكز على منظومة متكاملة تجمع البحث العلمي، والنمذجة الأولية، والتوجيه، والتمويل، والملكية الفكرية، والشراكات الصناعية، والوصول إلى الأسواق. وتوصي الدراسة ببناء مسار مؤسسي واضح يربط البحث بالابتكار والتجسيد التجاري والأثر المجتمعي.الكلمات المفتاحية: جامعة الجيل الرابع؛ شركات ناشئة؛ ذكاء اصطناعي؛ ريادة أعمال جامعية؛ الجامعة التقنية الدنماركية.Abstract: This exploratory study examines how a Fourth-Generation University can move beyond knowledge production towards transforming research and technology into startups and societal value, with particular attention to artificial intelligence. Using DTU as a single case, the study applies a descriptive-analytical approach based on documentary induction and content analysis of DTU and DTU Skylab annual reports, official webpages, programmes and published evidence on startups, funding, prototyping, technology transfer and AI. The evidence shows that DTU supported 399 startup teams in 2024 and that DTU students and employees incorporated 120 new startups. Investment in DTU startups increased from DKK 0.7 billion in 2020 to DKK 2.6 billion in 2024.The study finds that startup creation is supported by an integrated ecosystem combining research, prototyping, coaching, funding, intellectual property, industry partnerships and market access. AI is embedded in this ecosystem through dedicated productization activities and research-based spinouts. The study recommends that universities seeking to become Fourth-Generation Universities build integrated innovation ecosystems and a clear pathway from research to prototype, intellectual property, funding, startup creation and market impact.Keywords: Fourth-Generation University; Startups; Artificial Intelligence; University Entrepreneurship; Technical University of Denmark (DTU).Résumé : Cette étude exploratoire vise à analyser comment l'université de quatrième génération évolue au-delà de son rôle traditionnel de production de connaissances pour valoriser les résultats de la recherche scientifique et de la technologie à travers la création de start-up et la génération d'une valeur ajoutée pour la société, avec une attention particulière portée à l'intelligence artificielle. documents.abstract: Simulators play a crucial role in the aerospace industry, ranging from simple desktop models to advanced Level D simulators used for pilot training. While most non-gaming simulators focus on crew training and client illustration, there is a notable deficiency in simulators that assist with cockpit design. Current methods primarily utilize standard CAD/CAE software alongside Digital Human Models, which often lack adequate functionality for comprehensive human factor evaluation for design optimization. This paper introduces a configurable Virtual Reality Spacecraft Simulator that is calibrated with data from microgravity studies from the International Space Station collected from two astronauts. The VR simulator is also integrated with human factor evaluation suit like eye gaze and EEG trackers. The proposed VR simulator implements immersive task execution in scenarios such as deorbiting manoeuvres, emergency responses, and robotic arm operations, while also comparing task completion times in microgravity conditions. Three applications of the VR spacecraft simulator are presented to highlight prospectives uses for informed design decisions.

Industries often hold valuable data locked in silos, limiting both the amount and diversity of data available for training machine learning models and consequently reducing accuracy and generalization capabilities. Centralizing sensitive data or sharing it with third parties introduces significant privacy and security risks, complicating data governance and control. Federated Learning (FL) addresses these challenges by enabling collaborative model training without the need to transfer raw data, thus preserving privacy while harnessing distributed information. Complementarily, Data Spaces provide a secure framework for trusted data exchange through standardized protocols and robust governance, ensuring interoperability and responsible data use. By integrating FL within a Data Space, organizations can overcome the dual hurdles of data silos and stringent privacy requirements, while FL inherently safeguards privacy by enabling collaborative model training without raw data transfer, its integration within a Data Space offers enhanced security and governance beyond traditional FL. This approach ensures that all interactions, from service discovery to model exchange, are governed by explicit policies and contracts, providing unprecedented traceability and control over the collaborative AI lifecycle. This paper presents a novel architecture implemented within the Mondragon-X Industrial Data Space that seamlessly embeds the FL workflow. Leveraging advanced EDC connectors, dedicated APIs, and the Flower AI framework in a hybrid edge-cloud environment, our approach enables continuous model updates, collaborative improvements, and strict data sovereignty, thereby establishing a scalable foundation for developing powerful and privacy-preserving industrial artificial intelligence (AI) solutions.
