documents.abstract: Grain boundaries (GBs) in polycrystalline Ni-based alloys strongly influence mechanical strength and fracture behavior, yet the effect of alloying elements such as Fe and Cr on GB cohesion remains difficult to quantify systematically. Using density functional theory (DFT), we compute rigid-body separation (RBS) curves for six symmetric-tilt Ni GBs, extracting the work of separation $W_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and maximum traction $σ_{\max}$ via the universal binding energy relation (UBER). We find that substitution of Cr or Fe into the GB plane increases both quantities relative to pure Ni GBs. To overcome the size limitations of DFT, we compare several machine-learning interatomic potential (MLIP) foundation models against the DFT dataset and identify a model achieving quantitative agreement with DFT for $W_{\mathrm{sep}}$ and $σ_{\max}$. This MLIP enables systematic sampling of alloying configurations at finer concentration steps. We show that alloying-induced changes in GB cohesion depend on both, element type and local structures, revealing trends that are inaccessible with DFT alone. Extending the analysis to a ternary $\mathrm{Ni}_{56}\mathrm{Fe}_{20}\mathrm{Cr}_{24}$ composition, inspired by the principal constituents of the widely used commercial Alloy 718, shows that the binary trends provide a useful basis for interpreting the combined effect of both substitutes, while explicit ternary calculations are required to capture their interplay quantitatively. Together, these results provide a validated workflow for quantifying the effect of alloying elements on GB cohesion in multicomponent alloys. The resulting values may serve as input for continuum-scale fracture models, paving the way toward atomistically informed multiscale modeling.

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.

The interpretation of neutron scattering data remains a major bottleneck in materials discovery, as it demands an iterative cycle of data reduction, modeling, and refinement. That is too time-consuming for experts and too complex for novices. Here we introduce DrSai-Rongzai, an autonomous agent built on a large language model (LLM) that perfoms joint neutron powder diffraction (NPD) and pair-distribution-function (PDF) analysis without human intervention. Deployed at the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS), the agent orchestrates established refinement software through a hierarchical “Reasoning + Acting” framework. Its core innovation, Agentic Context Operation (ACO), maintains a coherent ‘working memory’ of file paths, intermediate results, and domain-specific rules across entire processing steps, even when the underlying large language model undergoes context compression. Across reference materials (Si, CsAgTe and Bi2MoO6), the agent refined structural parameters statistically indistinguishable from expert-derived solutions, while requiring markedly fewer iterative cycles. In an exhaustive 18-run factorial ablation study on two high-entropy alloys, we systematically evaluated the MemoWrite and CoreSkillWrite in ACO mechanisms with and without 50k-token context compression, quantifying the necessity of each component. Memo improved both mean composite performance and repeatability even without compression (+ 20.2% and + 11.3%, respectively). Under compression, Memo improved these metrics by + 10.7% and + 17.0%, and retaining CoreSkill provided a further + 12.5% and + 6.6% improvement, yielding a mean composite score of 0.9316 and repeatability stability of 0.9905 for full ACO. The agent is integrated with a permission-controlled CSNS data interface, enabling secure, on-demand analysis of user-proprietary data with automatic archiving. By combining rigorous benchmarking with practical, facility-ready deployment, DrSai-Rongzai demonstrates that autonomous AI agents can move beyond assisted recommendations to become reliable partners in complex structural science, potentially accelerating the rate of discovery at pulsed neutron sources worldwide.

documents.abstract: This study presents an intelligent decision support system (IDSS) that integrates the extreme gradient boosting algorithm with the six-mechanism risk governance framework, which covers identification, assessment, warning, prevention, response, and accountability, for large-scale water diversion projects. Using real-time data from Internet of Things sensors, hazard logs, and management records, the system enables dynamic risk classification and interpretable early warning. Implemented in the Oujiang Water Diversion Project, the IDSS improves the timeliness of decision-making, strengthens proactive risk response, and supports the closed-loop tracking of high-risk events through human–AI collaboration. The paper also discusses practical limitations and provides guidance for deploying similar IDSSs in public infrastructure contexts.

Transparency mode is an important feature of modern hearable devices, enabling real-time reproduction of environmental sounds while preserving perceptual comfort and situational awareness. Conventional transparency pipelines rely on static filtering and fixed loudness control, which perform poorly in highly non-stationary acoustic environments and often produce perceptual harshness, clipping, and unstable loudness behaviour. This paper presents an initial, proof-of-concept investigation into a low-complexity hybrid adaptive transparency architecture that integrates statistically driven loudness control, content-aware filtering, and lightweight acoustic feature analysis. Short-time energy and spectral centroid are jointly used to detect perceptually harsh high-frequency events and classify incoming acoustic frames. Based on this classification, harsh events are selectively attenuated through targeted band-stop filtering, while benign ambient sounds are preserved through gentle low-pass filtering. Loudness stability is addressed using an adaptive RMS-based limiter that dynamically updates its threshold via a combination of exponential moving average and percentile-based ambient estimators; this is a statistically driven loudness control strategy rather than a validated psychoacoustic loudness model. The proposed system is implemented in a real-time MATLAB framework that reflects the constraints of hearable-class digital signal processing. On a limited set of real-world environmental recordings, the proposed system shows lower peak-to-average ratio, improved transient handling, faster recovery, and smoother loudness trajectories compared to three static transparency baselines implemented for this study, alongside computational characteristics compatible with embedded hearable devices: an estimated per-hop cost of approximately 9000 multiply-accumulate operations. These findings are indicative rather than conclusive. This is a preliminary framework: perceptual evaluation was conducted informally by the two authors only, without an independent listener panel or a formal psychoacoustic loudness/sharpness model beyond the offline metrics reported, and the evaluation corpus was limited in size and diversity. Formal subjective validation and larger-scale, independently annotated evaluation are identified as essential next steps before broader claims can be supported.

As we move from Industry 4.0 to Industry 5.0, fully automated systems start to give way to human-centric ones, in which human traits such as creativity and problem solving are leveraged and augmented through AI assistance. Human-AI collaboration is therefore fundamental. However, industrial processes are becoming increasingly complex. They are now hyper-connected ecosystems, integrating IIoT, AI, robotics or digital twins with new data streams and interdependencies. For a human, extracting and analyzing data from this complex ecosystem so that informed decisions can be taken becomes a non-trivial challenge. In this paper, we propose an agent-based architecture to interact with a Digital Twin, using FlexSim and a middleware layer as an interface. By leveraging the natural language understanding capabilities of LLMs, the system enables users to interact with the Digital Twin through intuitive, complex queries, democratizing access to data-driven insights and empowering human decision-making. A representative case study is used to provide an early validation of the middleware layer.

documents.abstract: Programmable Radio Access Networks (RANs) enable runtime deployment of traffic-control functions, but selecting the appropriate configuration remains challenging as network conditions and service requirements change over time. Conventional solutions often rely on static rules or learning-based controllers with predefined state and action spaces, limiting their ability to accommodate changing intents. This paper introduces an LLM-driven xApp for traffic control in programmable RANs. The proposed architecture combines operator-defined service intents, runtime E2 interface telemetry, and the currently deployed configuration to generate traffic-management policies without blocking packet forwarding or the processing of incoming E2 measurements during LLM inference. Experiments on an OpenAirInterface 5G environment show that the proposed controller dynamically adapts the traffic-control pipeline to runtime intent changes, achieving an average intent satisfaction ratio of 0.91, compared with 0.52 for a static TC-RAN configuration. When channel conditions degrade, the controller maintains an intent satisfaction ratio of approx. 0.88, compared with approx. 0.4 for the static baseline.

documents.abstract: Explainability in diffusion-based 3D generative models remains limited, as their black-box nature obscures how complex geometric structures emerge from noise. Conventional post-hoc attribution methods, while useful for discriminative tasks, fail to capture the iterative, dynamic evolution intrinsic to the reverse diffusion process. We introduce Manifold Diffusion Explanation (MDE), a novel intrinsic framework that reinterprets denoising as traversable semantic paths along the Riemannian manifold of the latent space. By tracking and visualizing these geodesic trajectories—from isotropic Gaussian noise to coherent 3D objects (e.g., chairs, airplanes)—we demonstrate that object-specific generation is directly encoded in the manifold’s curvature and geodesic structure. This path-centric view yields transparent-by-design explanations rooted in the model’s internal dynamics, bypassing the need for external surrogates or post-hoc approximations. MDE thus bridges high-fidelity 3D generation with mechanistic interpretability, providing deeper insight into how diffusion models encode and unfold geometric priors. Our approach opens new avenues for trustworthy, human-aligned 3D generative AI in safety-critical domains.

documents.abstract: Purpose – This study aims to analyse the business models and development strategies of two small-scale egg-laying chicken farms, namely UD Golden Egg Farm and UD Amanah Farm, located in Talok Village, Tegal Regency, Central Java. Originality - The novelty of this study lies in the application of an integrative approach between BMC and SWOT Analysis to analyse two small-scale smallholder livestock business units with different management characteristics. Methode – This study uses a descriptive qualitative approach with the main methods of in-depth interviews, field observations, and documentation. The analysis was conducted in two stages, namely the Business Model Canvas (BMC) to map the nine main elements of the business model (customer segments, value propositions, distribution channels, customer relationships, revenue streams, key resources, key activities, key partners, and cost structure) and SWOT analysis to assess the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, and threats of the business. Finding – The results of the study show that UD Golden Egg Farm excels in conventional production efficiency, cost control, and income diversification through the processing of waste into organic fertiliser, while UD Amanah Farm is more advanced in terms of marketing digitalisation, community-based customer management, and partnerships with the Free Nutritious Meals (MBG) programme. SWOT analysis identifies the main strengths as the application of Occupational Health and Safety (OHS) principles, energy efficiency, and workforce flexibility, while the weaknesses lie in the limitations of the cage security and biosecurity systems. Development opportunities include the application of appropriate technology (automatic sensors and digital recording systems) and diversification towards a circular economy based on livestock waste. The main threats include predators, climate change, and poultry diseases that can reduce productivity. The combination of BMC and SWOT analyses shows that the integration of conventional production efficiency and digital innovation can be a model for sustainable poultry agribusiness (integrated sustainable agribusiness) for smallholder farms in rural areas. Limitations and Implications – This study is limited to SWOT and BMC analyses, so the results cannot be widely generalised. The implications of this study can serve as a reference for the development of small-scale livestock business models that are adaptive to changes in technology, the environment, and market dynamics.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), including large language models, retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), and multi-agent systems, is used both as a tool around the medical device lifecycle and, less often, inside devices. These uses should not be conflated. This scoping review characterises current applications in design, regulatory management, maintenance, and risk assessment, and identifies where published evidence is thinnest. PubMed, IEEE Xplore, Scopus, and arXiv were searched for 2022–2026 studies applying GenAI to hardware devices, SaMD, or medical wearables. Sixty-one studies were charted with the population–concept–context framework and mapped to the four pillars. Most included work is experimental. Reports cluster in regulatory document analysis and in risk or cybersecurity modelling. Live maintenance and generative hardware design remain sparse in this search. RAG and agent pipelines are commonly used to ground outputs, but published metrics are task-specific and do not demonstrate automated MDR or FDA compliance. GenAI can assist retrieval and drafting across the lifecycle, yet longitudinal real-world validation and human-in-the-loop controls are still scarce. In this corpus, operationally validated maintenance and in-device safety systems are the thin end of the map, not another document-mining prototype.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.

This article presents a methodological proposal grounded in Project-Based Learning (PBL), implemented in secondary education, with the aim of strengthening students’ intrinsic motivation, participation, and deep learning. The study was developed from a qualitative approach through participatory action research, which made it possible to analyze and transform the traditional pedagogical practices of seven teachers in a public educational institution located in a municipality in Colombia. The experience was structured in four phases: diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation. The results show an increase in student motivation, greater cooperation among teachers, and a reduction in failure rates. Likewise, the findings indicate that PBL fosters the satisfaction of basic psychological needs—autonomy, competence, and relatedness—which are essential foundations of human motivation and enhance deep learning, knowledge transfer, and school persistence. Consequently, PBL emerges as a relevant pedagogical strategy for promoting holistic and humanizing education, capable of connecting knowledge with students’ real and meaningful contexts.

Relevance. Software systems that process sensitive data are designed on the assumption that every component performs a predefined operation after an authorisation check. An artificial intelligence (AI) agent, in which a large language model (LLM) selects and calls tools autonomously, does not satisfy this assumption: each decision is made by a probabilistic model based on text, part of which comes from unverified sources. In applications that integrate an LLM, the clear separation of data from instructions disappears. In the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications 2025, prompt injection is ranked first and excessive agency is a separate risk.

Team performance has been extensively theorized in military, healthcare, sports, and organizational domains, yet the extent to which these theories transfer to cyber teams has not been systematically established. Through a systematic review of traditional team performance research and a structured comparison to the current cyber-team evidence, this study addresses that gap. We followed PRISMA 2020 guidance and extracted data from 267 primary studies published between 2015 and 2025 across organizational, project, sports, health care, military and technology-mediated team settings comprising 798 relationship records and 644 unique factor-pair associations spanning 60 standardized factors. The resulting factor inventory and relationship network were then compared against a published set of 42 cyber-team factors using a five-category correspondence rubric, which two coders applied independently (κ = 0.78 for cross-corpus mapping; κ = 0.84 for extraction). Findings demonstrate broad convergence at the factor level: communication, coordination, leadership, trust, shared mental models, and cohesion show strong conceptual correspondence across the traditional and cyber-team literatures, although their operational forms vary with technological mediation, temporal pressure, distributed work, and adversarial conditions. Several well-established traditional-team constructs remain underrepresented in cyber-team research. We integrate these results into a four-layer associative pathway model organizing structural inputs, mediating processes, emergent states, and multidimensional outcomes, and use it to identify where cyber-team theory should extend rather than replace traditional team science. Because the cyber comparison base is weighted toward software engineering, findings are most directly applicable to cyber-relevant technical teams but require further testing in security operations, incident response, and human–AI teaming contexts.

Artificial intelligence is no longer an experimental idea in Washington; it has entered everyday federal administration. Commercial vendors build the underlying models and data centers, while federal agencies act as buyers, users, and regulators. This paper examines how the federal government adopts AI, how private vendors shape that process, and how policy approaches shifted between the Biden and Trump administrations. While the Biden administration emphasized civil rights, risk mitigation, and structured safeguards (Executive Order 14110; OMB M-24-10), the Trump administration shifted the focus toward rapid deployment, regulatory relief, and commercial competitiveness (Executive Order 14179; OMB M-25-21). Drawing on public administration concepts like the principal-agent dilemma, vendor lock-in, and administrative burden, this study reviews real deployments across payment integrity, clinical documentation, drug review, and national security. The central lesson is that buying commercial software does not automatically create public value. To build an AI policy that supports both ordinary citizens and private enterprise, the federal government needs in-house technical capacity, open procurement standards to prevent vendor monopolies, practical testing based on real staff workflows, and clear administrative due process for the public.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Problem definition: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) is revolutionizing production and operational models, yet whether and how AI technologies diffuse across economically linked firms, especially partners along supply chains, remains underexplored. Methodology/results: This paper documents the diffusion of AI technologies along supply chains where principal customers’ AI adoption significantly predicts dependent suppliers’ subsequent adoption. We establish the causal effect of this diffusion through rigorous and comprehensive empirical strategies that address endogeneity concerns, including placebo tests, selection tests, and an identification strategy based on the random H-1B visa lottery outcome. The diffusion mechanism is primarily driven by learning rather than catering, with suppliers acquiring specific AI applications from customers. The learning effect is stronger in relationships with higher relationship-specific investments and more frequent interactions. Suppliers experiencing AI diffusion achieve substantial economic benefits through quality improvement and cost reduction. Managerial implications: For corporate managers, our findings demonstrate that supply chain relationships serve as critical conduits for building AI capabilities, particularly for resource-constrained smaller suppliers, highlighting the strategic value of cultivating partnerships with technologically advanced firms. For policymakers, our results reveal supply chains as natural mechanisms for democratizing AI access, suggesting that policies supporting supply chain integration and knowledge sharing could accelerate the broader diffusion of AI benefits across the economy and society.

documents.abstract: The relevance of the study is due to the fact that the emerging information (digital) technologies, which are now an inevitable reality, have an impact on both society as a whole and the individual modern person, and in many cases have already become part of the latter's daily life. This process is manifested, among other things, in the widespread use of digital technologies, neural networks, intelligent systems, and so on. Artificial intelligence (AI) occupies a special place in this list. Today, there is hardly any area of society or human activity that is not affected by this technological advancement. This also applies to the legal sphere, one of the sections of which is the field of human and civil rights and freedoms. Taking into account the above, the goal of the research can be defined as a comprehensive analysis of all aspects related to: 1) the use of artificial intelligence in various spheres of the state and society; 2) the observance of human and civil rights in the context of the diverse and multifaceted use of AI as a factor influencing the observance of human and civil rights and freedoms both at the domestic and international levels. During our research, we concluded that it is necessary to create a clear regulatory framework that will ensure a balance between the use of AI, on the one hand, and the protection of public interests, as well as human and civil rights and freedoms, on the other. An example of such a framework, in particular, could be the legal regulation of artificial intelligence. By means of the said regulation, it is necessary to keep the process of using AI in various fields and spheres under constant control, and this process itself must be approached very carefully (as is the case with any achievement of scientific and technological progress): 1) to avoid the occurrence of negative consequences and side effects, 2) with the aim of clearly appropriate boundaries of the said use, 3) so that AI truly becomes a real assistant to humans, and not a substitute for human intelligence.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Optimal sensor placement determines which measurements can support reconstruction, identification, diagnosis, or control under practical limits on instrumentation. This critical review examines methodological developments in machine learning, Artificial Intelligence, and model order reduction from 2016 to October 2026, giving priority to papers that establish or substantially extend selection principles. A common measurement and task formulation connects sparse discriminant sensing, reduced-basis reconstruction, pivoted orthogonal–triangular matrix factorization (QR), surrogate-assisted optimization, and reinforcement learning. A flowchart shows how these approaches can combine representations, objectives, and selection procedures. The analysis shows how representation error, observation noise, target sensitivity, and physical constraints affect the optimal layout. Comparative tables separate the contributions of the objective, representation, selector, and estimator. Applications illustrate these differences in physical systems. Simulation, retrospective subsets of measured data, and implemented sparse networks provide different levels of validation. Research priorities include calibrated uncertainty under deployment shift, feasible layouts, benchmarks that isolate placement gains from estimator capacity, and physical validation under realistic failure and life cycle costs.

In vitro fertilization treatments are still inefficient with only a 60% probability for achieving pregnancy in the first embryo transfer attempt when embryos are euploid. Then, optimizing endometrial diagnosis is one of the main strategies for avoiding the loss of embryos during this inefficient process. In the last years, a new kind of non-timing endometrial failure has been proposed as an idiopathic cause of infertility strongly associated with poor reproductive outcomes. However, effective therapeutic options for treating the endometrium remain lacking, underscoring the need for new personalized treatments that reduce the number of attempts needed for achieving live birth. This multicentre prospective study included 192 endometrial biopsies in mid-secretory phase from patients undergoing In vitro fertilization. Patients were classified as good/poor prognosis endotypes, and next subdivided in subendotypes, according to reproductive success and transcriptomic profiles using machine learning. Therapeutic drugs capable of reversing these molecular subendotypes were identified using system pharmacology approaches. The potential effect in endometrium of selected drugs was validated in human endometrial stromal cell lines through RT-PCR, F-actin staining, and enzyme-linked immunosorbent assays. The poor-prognosis endotype ( n = 43) was associated with lower pregnancy (26.3%vs.66.0%, p = 1.99 × 10 − 5 ) and live birth (40.0%vs.87.1%, p = 0.0013), higher biochemical (30.3%vs.7.2%, p = 0.0372), and clinical miscarriage rates (42.9%vs.6.2%, p = 0.0159) when compared to good-prognosis endotype. This poor-prognosis endotype was subdivided into two molecular subendotypes, one associated with increased biochemical miscarriage rate ( n = 16; 66.7%vs.14.3%, p = 0.0022,), and the other with increased clinical miscarriage rate ( n = 27, 50%vs.0%, p = 0.0001), when compared between them, both of them characterized by abnormal decidualization features. Additionally, biochemical miscarriage subendotype highlighted also immune dysregulation as a key biological process. In silico drug prioritization identified genistein, pioglitazone, alprostadil, flunisolide, and tenoxicam as approved drugs with the potential to reverse the molecular signatures of these subendotypes. In vitro validation in endometrial stromal cells showed genistein and pioglitazone promoting decidualization, whereas alprostadil, flunisolide, and tenoxicam inhibiting well-known biomarkers of immune response, supporting their potential therapeutic role for endometrial failure. We have proposed for the first time potential drugs for an idiopathic endometrial non-timing infertility that could reduce attempts needed for achieving live birth, although further validations in patients are required towards personalised medicine. Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a leading cause of global cancer-related mortality, driven by an ongoing etiological shift toward metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD). While early detection is vital for curative intervention, traditional surveillance and diagnostic modalities offer limited sensitivity due to operator dependence and inter-observer variability. This narrative review provides a comprehensive synthesis of emerging and investigational artificial intelligence (AI) applications across different stages of HCC management, ranging from research-stage predictive models to AI-assisted clinical tools. AI-driven radiomics workflows convert complex, non-invasive imaging profiles into high-dimensional data, enhancing the preoperative prediction of microvascular invasion (MVI) and refining standardized Liver Imaging Reporting and Data System (LI-RADS) classifications. Complementing radiology, computational pathology leverages deep learning and emerging pathological foundation models to standardize oncological scoring, mitigate inter-observer variability, and automate histological tumor segmentation. Multimodal AI fusion networks further bridge macroscopic imaging phenotypes with microscopic pathomic signatures and molecular profiles. At the population level, machine learning algorithms optimize dynamic surveillance by integrating longitudinal clinical data with liquid biopsy biomarkers, with the aim of detecting molecular change before it becomes visible on imaging. This review additionally examines AI integration within prospective clinical trial frameworks, encompassing endpoint standardization, patient stratification, and treatment response prediction. While technical challenges including scanner variability and retrospective validation gaps persist, explainable AI (XAI) and federated learning represent the next critical frontier for establishing transportable, accountable digital oncology workflows. Most current applications remain at the technical-validation stage and come largely from single-center, retrospective cohorts. Externally validated models are fewer, and evidence that AI improves clinical decisions or patient outcomes is still very limited.

documents.abstract: Men who have sex with men (MSM) remain disproportionately affected by human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), with persistent gaps in prevention, testing, and treatment across selected stages of the HIV care continuum. Artificial intelligence (AI) offers emerging opportunities to support HIV-related services; however, evidence of its application in MSM populations remains limited and fragmented. This study aims to systematically examine emerging evidence on AI applications across selected stages of the HIV care continuum. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses 2020 guidelines, this systematic review was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (CRD420261292658) on 25 January 2026. It included studies published between 2015 and 2025 that examined MSM and evaluated AI-enabled tools across the HIV care continuum. PubMed and Scopus were searched using structured terms. Two reviewers independently screened studies, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (using the Joanna Briggs Institute and Mixed Methods Appraisal Checklist). Evidence was synthesized narratively. Ten studies from diverse global settings were included. AI applications included machine learning, deep learning, network-based models, and chatbot systems. Predictive models showed promising performance for specific tasks, including HIV risk prediction, Pre exposure prophylaxis adherence prediction, sexual-risk classification, and clinic-attendance forecasting. Evidence for AI-enabled interventions was more limited. Chatbot-based interventions primarily demonstrated feasibility and acceptability, while influencer-identification approaches were evaluated using behavioural or testing-related outcomes, with mixed findings. Overall, evidence demonstrating sustained improvements in clinical or population-level HIV outcomes was limited. AI-enabled tools demonstrated promising predictive performance and potential utility for supporting selected HIV prevention and care activities among MSM. However, evidence of real-world effectiveness in improving behavioural, clinical, or service-delivery outcomes remains limited. Further prospective studies, external validation, and real-world implementation evaluations across diverse populations and settings are needed before conclusions regarding clinical or public health effectiveness can be established.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: BACKGROUND When students perceive artificial intelligence (AI) as a threat to their career prospects (an environmental factor), this perception may elicit self-doubt (a cognitive factor), which in turn may lead to avoidance of academic challenges (a behavioral response), ultimately contributing to anxiety or depression (psychological outcomes). However, to date, the literature lacks empirical evidence supporting this viewpoint within university student samples. AIM To explore the associations between multidimensional AI attitudes and mental health outcomes among Chinese university students, and to examine the nonlinear relationships and the mediating role of self-efficacy in these associations. METHODS A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 2736 undergraduate students from China. Linear regression, restricted cubic spline (RCS) analysis, and path analysis were applied to examine the relationships between AI attitudes (anxiety, job insecurity, self-doubt, and procrastination), self-efficacy, and mental health outcomes (anxiety, depression, stress, loneliness, suicidal ideation, and non-suicidal self-injury). RESULTS Students’ AI attitudes showed a differentiated structure, characterized by low anxiety (9.5%), high job insecurity (50.4%), and moderate levels of self-doubt (25.6%) and procrastination (36.8%). All four AI attitude dimensions positively predicted poor mental health, with procrastination emerging as the strongest predictor. The RCS analysis revealed heterogeneous nonlinear relationships: AI-related anxiety showed nonlinearity for most outcomes, self-doubt and procrastination only for severe outcomes, while job insecurity exhibited stable linearity. Path analysis confirmed that self-efficacy played a partial mediating role in the AI attitude-mental health link. CONCLUSION AI attitudes are associated with complex linear and nonlinear impacts on university students’ mental health, with self-efficacy serving as a key mediating mechanism. These correlational findings provide an empirical reference for targeted mental health interventions and AI literacy education in higher education settings.

documents.abstract: Neglected tropical diseases (NTDs) affect more than one billion people globally, disproportionately burdening populations in low-resource tropical and subtropical settings. Recent advances in artificial intelligence (AI) offer considerable opportunities to strengthen NTD control, yet the scope, maturity, and translational readiness of AI applications across this disease portfolio remain incompletely characterized. We conducted a systematic review of peer-reviewed studies applying AI methods to NTD-related problems, searching multiple databases using predefined strategies and screening studies against explicit inclusion and exclusion criteria. Data were extracted on disease focus, AI methodology, data modalities, validation strategies, performance metrics, and implementation context. Thematic analyses were performed to characterize research trends, geographic distribution, and research priorities. Reporting followed PRISMA guidelines. We identified a rapidly expanding but uneven body of literature spanning 289 studies, dominated by applications in disease diagnosis (40.1%), prognosis (17.7%), surveillance (15.2%), outbreak prediction (13.5%), treatment monitoring (7.3%), and drug discovery (6.2%). Over 70% of studies employed supervised machine learning or deep learning applied to imaging, clinical, or epidemiological data. Performance was frequently reported using discrimination metrics, while calibration, external validation, and prospective evaluation remained uncommon. Research activity is concentrated in a small number of countries and institutions, notably Brazil and India, with limited representation from other highly endemic regions, particularly sub-Saharan Africa and South-East Asia. Only a minority of studies addressed considerations critical for real-world deployment, including data governance, health system integration, explainability, fairness, and interpretability. AI holds substantial promise for supporting NTD control and elimination, but the current evidence base reveals important methodological, geographic, and translational gaps. Future research should prioritize robust validation, transparent reporting, equity-aware design, and meaningful engagement with endemic-country stakeholders. Coordinated investment in data infrastructure, capacity building, and governance frameworks will be essential if AI-enabled innovations are to translate into sustainable public health impact for the populations most affected by NTDs.

This study examined artificial intelligence integration and its relationship with self-rated instructional planning and assessment construction competency among public elementary school teachers in Zone III, Division of Zambales. A descriptive–correlational survey involved 155 teachers from 12 schools in Cabangan, San Felipe, San Narciso, and San Antonio during school year 2025–2026. Schools were purposively selected, and eligible teachers were included through total enumeration. A researcher-made questionnaire underwent expert review and pilot reliability testing. Descriptive statistics, Mann–Whitney tests, one-way analysis of variance, and Pearson correlations were used. Teachers rated themselves highly competent in instructional planning (mean = 3.65) and assessment construction (mean = 3.59). Artificial intelligence was highly integrated in planning (mean = 3.30) and moderately integrated in assessment construction (mean = 3.02). Learning materials received the highest planning integration rating, while feedback received the lowest assessment rating. Planning and assessment competencies were strongly correlated (r = .823, p < .001). Planning-related artificial intelligence use showed small positive associations with planning competency (r = .180–.249). Use for creating assessments and designing rubrics was significantly associated with assessment competency, but use for analyzing results and providing feedback was not. Selected differences occurred across educational attainment, position, and compensation groups. The findings support professional learning focused on differentiation, assessment review, and feedback. They do not establish that artificial intelligence improves teacher competency. A proposed action plan offers a basis for further implementation and evaluation.

The advent of the era of artificial intelligence (AI) has brought unprecedented opportunities and challenges to anesthesia nursing. We aimed to investigate the status of AI literacy of anesthesia nurses and analyze its associated factors. In March 2025, anesthesia nurses from 34 hospitals in southwest China were selected as the participants of a multicenter cross-sectional survey and were investigated with the AI literacy questionnaire based on the literature, the Nursing Informatics Competency Scale and the Chinese version of the Critical Thinking Diagnostic for Frontline Nurses. Data from 671 nurses were analyzed. Questionnaire structure was examined with exploratory and confirmatory factor analyses in split halves, and associated factors with hierarchical regression using a priori covariates and cluster-robust standard errors. Overall, 503 (75.0%) of the anesthesia nurses had used AI tools. The mean AI literacy item score was 3.79 on a 1–5 scale, between “neutral” and “agree”. The four-factor model fitted well (CFI = 0.995), but parallel analysis suggested three factors without a separate AI awareness factor, and the dimensions were not clearly distinct. After adjustment for individual, professional and organizational characteristics (Model 3), previous AI training ( B = 6.58, 95% CI 4.72 to 8.44), more frequent AI use and a higher professional title were associated with higher AI literacy. A master’s degree or above and working in a hospital below Grade IIIA (imprecisely estimated) were associated with lower AI literacy. Further adding nursing informatics competence and critical thinking (Model 4) increased R ² by 0.224 (adjusted R ² = 0.776), and the overall association with AI-use frequency was attenuated. AI literacy met the heterotrait–monotrait criterion against both scales but not the Fornell–Larcker criterion against nursing informatics competence (latent r = 0.84). Professional title and AI training are factors associated with the AI literacy of anesthesia nurses. The associations with nursing informatics competence and critical thinking may partly reflect shared self-report variance. Nursing managers could formulate targeted training programs for nurses’ AI literacy based on these associated factors. These cross-sectional findings do not demonstrate that training improves AI literacy. Not applicable.

documents.abstract: AI is viewed as a tool that is suitable for SMEs, however, it might not be feasible unless SMEs have the technological, organizational, human and environmental conditions to enable its implementation. This study investigates how to define AI readiness and its contribution to explaining the adoption of AI within the SME context in Bangladesh. 310 SME decision makers responded and provided valid answers to the survey. Structural equation modelling was used to test the proposed model. Results of the measurement models showed good model fit, factor loadings, internal consistency, convergent validity, and discriminant validity. Fit of the structural model was also excellent. Within the four constructs, technological readiness, organisational readiness, human-capital readiness, and environmental readiness all had positive and statistically significant impacts on overall AI readiness. An overall high AI readiness positively affected the adoption of AI. Another mediation analysis revealed that overall, AI readiness was a significant mediator of all four dimensions of readiness and adoption. Overall, AI readiness and AI adoption was explained by 53.2% and 45.4% of the variance in the model, respectively. The results clearly identify that the-AI readiness factor serves as a pivotal central organisational mechanism that transforms resources, capabilities, people, and conditions into implementing AI in operations. The research provides a comprehensive approach for SME digital transformation in emerging economies.

documents.abstract: The article examines the application of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in web analytics and their role in improving business management in the digital economy. The study aims to systematize practical approaches to AI integration into analytical processes and identify promising directions for their further development. The main applications of AI in web analytics are classified, including data collection and processing, user segmentation, behavioral and sales forecasting, anomaly detection, personalization, and automated reporting. The advantages of AI implementation are identified, particularly increased analytical efficiency, improved forecasting accuracy, reduced human error, and enhanced data-driven decision-making. Key limitations related to data quality, privacy, information security, and ethical considerations are also highlighted. The study outlines future prospects for AI-driven web analytics, emphasizing the development of AI assistants capable of interpreting metrics, generating insights, and providing recommendations for marketing optimization and managerial decision-making.

Objective To map and synthesise existing evidence on computational summarisation technologies, including machine learning–based and natural language processing–based approaches, designed to generate multimodal (textual, visual, and audio) patient summaries of adult intensive care unit (ICU) stays. Materials and methods This scoping review followed Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and PRISMA-ScR guidance. Studies involving adults in any ICU setting and using artificial intelligence–enabled approaches to generate patient summaries were eligible. Searches were conducted across five major databases and grey literature sources. Two reviewers independently screened records. Data were extracted using a structured charting tool and independently verified by a second reviewer. Findings were synthesised using descriptive statistics and narrative synthesis. Results Eleven studies met inclusion criteria. Eight generated textual summaries, three produced visual outputs, and one developed an audio interface. Ten tools were clinician-facing; only one study generated summaries for families. Approaches included large language models, rule-based natural language generation, information extraction, trajectory modelling, and speech-based systems. No study implemented a fully multimodal summarisation system. All evaluations were conducted using retrospective data, simulations, or prototypes, with no prospective testing in live clinical workflows. Five themes emerged: predominance of text-based summarisation, early feasibility of large language models with reliability limitations, predominance of clinician-facing applications, heterogeneous evaluation practices, and limited evidence of clinical implementation. Conclusion Current ICU summarisation research demonstrates technical proof-of-concept feasibility but limited clinical readiness. Progress will require rigorous evaluation, stabilisation safeguards, and multimodal, patient- and family-centred designs capable of operating within regulatory and safety-critical clinical environments.

documents.abstract: This article explores creative processes involving composition students in higher music education and music artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Music composition, production, and recording have historically been receptive to technological advancements. In recent years, AI has permeated most aspects of society, and musical and educational practices are no exception to its influence. It has been contended that the potential benefits of AI technology are achieved at the expense of a loss of diversity, the devaluation of music professionals, and the black-boxing of the creative process in music composition. This article engages with posthumanist theory and Deleuze and Guattari’s concept diagram to unbox creative processes in music composition practices, reconfigured by technological developments. Four narratives with superimposed diagrammatic analyses of mapped workflows are presented, displaying the process of composing with AI as rhizomatic events contingent upon assemblages. From the diagrammatic analyses, some features of composing with AI are discerned. These features include increasing efficiency by both limiting virtual space and generating ideation space, collective proficiency for enhancing strengths and overcoming weaknesses, and distributed creative agency claiming assemblages as generators of novelty and value. The emphasis lies on differences in workflows, outputs, and learning when engaging with AI and technology. The discussion also points towards a reconfiguration of learning as unpredictable and diverse, inherent to, as well as among, protean subjects and suggesting a need for reconfigured educational and compositional proceedings in higher music education.

Large language models are increasingly deployed as LLM-as-a-Service (LLMaaS), where user queries are sent to remote LLMs for inference, raising severe privacy concerns about the exposure of sensitive user inputs. Differentially private inference mitigates these risks by injecting noise into input embeddings. However, existing methods struggle to balance privacy and utility, as stronger privacy protection often leads to substantial accuracy degradation in LLM inference. In this work, we propose DP-SPD, a differentially private LLM inference framework that protects user queries by hiding the real query among client-generated dummy queries. All queries are randomly shuffled before being sent to the server, preventing direct identification of the user's true intent. To improve inference efficiency, we exploit the shared-prefix structure among queries and reuse transformer key--value (KV) caches during decoding. We analyze the privacy guarantee of DP-SPD and evaluate its utility on classification and generation tasks, as well as its privacy protection under QIA, EIA, and GPT-based attacks. Experimental results show that our method achieves strong inference-time privacy protection and near-plaintext utility while improving inference efficiency through shared-prefix KV-cache reuse.

documents.abstract: Objectives: Peer review validates research findings and upholds the quality and credibility of scientific publications. This study aimed to assess the quality of peer-review reports generated by GPT-5.6, Claude Sonnet-4.6, and Google Gemini-3.1 Pro, while evaluating the same set of published scientific articles. Methodology: This comparative study was performed in the “Department of Physiology, College of Medicine, King Saud University, Riyadh, Saudi Arabia” from August 23, 2026, to September 10, 2026. In this study, 30 original published articles were identified, and each article was submitted to GPT-5.6 (n=30), Claude Sonnet-4.6 (n=30), and Google Gemini-3.1 Pro (n=30). Each AI model generated 30 individual review reports, for a total of 90 peer-review reports. A panel of five faculty members evaluated the peer-review reports, and each report was scored out of five marks. Each examiner evaluated peer-review reports generated by ChatGPT (30), Claude Sonnet (30), and Google Gemini (30). The frequencies, percentages, mean ± SEM and 95% CIs were calculated, and p-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.Results: AI models generated 90 peer-review reports, 30 each from ChatGPT, Claude Sonnet, and Google Gemini. Across the five examiners, ChatGPT received an overall grade of 634.1/750 (84.54%), Claude Sonnet received 690.4/750 (92.05%), and Google Gemini received 465.3/750 (62.04%). Claude’s Sonnet review reports received the highest grades, followed by ChatGPT and Google Gemini (p=0.001). Conclusions: The AI model, Claude Sonnet-4.6, produces significantly better review reports than GPT-5.6 and Google Gemini-3.1 Pro. These AI models summarize complex information and identify potential gaps, methodological concerns, and issues in the results and discussion sections of medical science articles. Integrating AI models within professional boundaries supports academic journals’ editorial workflows rather than replacing human peer review.

BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Addiction consult services (ACSs) increase inpatient treatment for opioid use disorder (OUD) and may support prescribing capacity among non-specialists. We evaluated whether cumulative provider-level ACS exposure was associated with independent buprenorphine initiation. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study of providers caring for hospitalized adults with OUD at an academic medical center (2018-2026). Providers entered at their first qualifying inpatient or emergency department encounter. Cumulative ACS exposure at initiation or censoring was categorized as 0, 1-2, 3-5, or ≥6 ACS-involved encounters. The outcome was time to first observed buprenorphine initiation during an encounter without an ACS consult. Sensitivity analyses examined consult-exposed providers, study-entry era, and exclusion of ED providers. RESULTS: Among 3,410 providers, 582 (17.1%) independently initiated buprenorphine. Compared with providers with no ACS exposure, providers with ≥6 exposures had a higher average rate of independent initiation (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR], 1.74; 95% CI, 1.40-2.16), whereas estimates for 1-2 and 3-5 exposures were not significant. Among consult-exposed providers, ≥6 versus 1-2 exposures was associated with a higher initiation rate (aHR, 1.78; 95% CI, 1.37-2.30). The association was present in both study-entry eras but not after excluding ED providers. DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS: High cumulative ACS exposure was associated with a higher average rate of subsequent independent buprenorphine initiation. The findings are consistent with workplace learning as one possible explanation for the observed associations. SCIENTIFIC SIGNIFICANCE: Repeated ACS exposure may identify opportunities for deliberate skill transfer, particularly among ED providers.

Background: Increased smartphone, tablet and laptop use among young adults has raised concerns about musculoskeletal discomfort and headaches. Prolonged screen use may involve sustained neck flexion, cervical muscle loading and visual strain. Aim: To assess the association of daily screen time with neck pain and headache frequency among hostel students. Methodology: This cross-sectional observational study included 130 hostel residents aged 18-25 years. Screen time was obtained from smartphone usage records. Neck pain was assessed using the Numeric Pain Rating Scale (NPRS), and headache frequency was recorded for the preceding four weeks. Spearman's correlation was used; p < 0.05 was considered significant. Results: Mean age was 20.60 ± 1.97 years and mean daily screen time was 4.10 ± 1.76 hours. Mean NPRS score was 1.99 ± 3.41 and mean headache score was 1.63 ± 3.42. Screen time had a weak positive correlation with neck pain (rho = 0.204, p = 0.020), but not headache frequency (rho = 0.035, p = 0.695). Conclusion: Screen time was weakly associated with neck pain, but not headache frequency. Ergonomic awareness, postural variation and regular breaks may help reduce screen-related discomfort.

Background/Objectives: Nurses’ medical artificial intelligence (AI)-based innovative behavior may contribute to the effective application of medical AI in clinical practice and the improvement of nursing care. This study examined whether medical explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) was indirectly associated with nurses’ medical AI-based innovative behavior through trust in medical AI and whether medical AI information disclosure moderated the association between medical XAI and trust in medical AI. Methods: A two-wave time-lagged survey with a two-month interval was conducted among 389 nurses from three hospitals in Anhui Province, China. Medical XAI and medical AI information disclosure were measured at Wave 1, whereas trust in medical AI and medical AI-based innovative behavior were measured at Wave 2. Mediation, moderation, and moderated mediation analyses were conducted using Hayes’ PROCESS macro (Models 4 and 7) with 5000 bootstrap resamples. Results: Medical XAI was positively associated with trust in medical AI (B = 0.28, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [0.20, 0.36], p < 0.001), which, in turn, was positively associated with medical AI-based innovative behavior (B = 0.24, SE = 0.05, 95% CI [0.14, 0.34], p < 0.001). The indirect association through trust in medical AI was significant (B = 0.07, BootSE = 0.02, 95% bootstrap CI [0.03, 0.10]). Medical AI information disclosure moderated the association between medical XAI and trust in medical AI (B = 0.08, SE = 0.04, 95% CI [0.01, 0.16], p < 0.05). Specifically, this association was not significant at a low level of medical AI information disclosure (B = 0.04, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [−0.07, 0.16], p > 0.05) but was positive at a high level (B = 0.16, SE = 0.06, 95% CI [0.04, 0.27], p < 0.01). The index of moderated mediation was significant (index = 0.02, BootSE = 0.01, 95% bootstrap CI [0.01, 0.05]). Conclusions: These preliminary findings suggest that trust in medical AI may represent a link between medical XAI and nurses’ medical AI-based innovative behavior and that this indirect association may be stronger at higher levels of medical AI information disclosure. Although the findings should be interpreted as associations rather than causal evidence, they may offer initial insights for technology providers, hospital administrators, and medical institutions.

documents.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) performs tasks once regarded as markers of human intelligence, how people judge the capacities of machines has become a question for intelligence research. This study examined perceived machine agency, the attribution of intelligence-related capacities such as thinking, planning, moral judgment, and problem solving to robots. We tested whether it is associated with psychological distress through AI anxiety and whether self-reported AI literacy moderates this pathway. A convenience sample of 1205 Chinese college students, mainly from Jiangsu Province, completed a cross-sectional survey. Controlling for gender, age, and subjective socioeconomic status, perceived machine agency was significantly but weakly associated with psychological distress. This association was indirect through AI anxiety, and the direct association was not significant. AI literacy significantly moderated the first stage of the indirect association, which became stronger as AI literacy increased. These cross-sectional findings describe associations rather than causal effects. They suggest that attributing intelligence-related capacities to machines is linked to students’ emotional well-being and that greater self-reported AI competence does not by itself weaken this link.

documents.abstract: Mobile autonomous robots are increasingly present in everyday environments, where their sounds play a key role in situational awareness and acceptance. Nevertheless, human responses to robot noise remain underexplored. This study examined how robot operating modes and added alerting sounds affect auditory localization and subjective ratings for a professional cleaning robot. Recordings of the robot operating at two velocities during cleaning and non-cleaning were presented. The non-cleaning mode was additionally combined with multi-tone and noise alerting signals, each with and without amplitude modulation. In a VR experiment with within-subjects design, 27 participants performed a localization task and rated annoyance, valence, arousal, and trustworthiness. Localization performance did not differ significantly between sound conditions. Exploratory post hoc analyses indicated that differences between sound conditions varied with participants’ general localization performance, yielding hypotheses for future studies on the role of baseline localization performance. The cleaning sound was rated as most annoying, least pleasant, and least trustworthy, whereas differences between the non-cleaning conditions were rather small. Overall, the alerting signals did not reliably improve localization under the present listening conditions, but some variants may nevertheless warrant further investigation due to their limited negative effects on subjective ratings.

Artificial intelligence for combinatorial optimization depends on high-quality, structured training data, yet transforming ambiguous natural-language descriptions into precise, executable formal models remains a major bottleneck, traditionally requiring extensive manual effort and domain expertise. We develop CPAM-LLM, an automated constraint-programming modeling framework based on large language models that converts unstructured problem specifications into validated and executable formal models. The framework integrates retrieval-augmented generation grounded in formal concept analysis for structural validation, chaos-mapping-based data augmentation to enhance cross-domain generalization, and dynamic constraint adaptation to accommodate evolving problem settings. We demonstrate its effectiveness across five scenarios, including DNA sequence design, reconfigurable energy storage systems, and unmanned vehicle logistics. The results show that the framework can automate the data-to-model pipeline while adapting reliably to changing requirements, providing a practical approach to automated data formalization and indicating the importance of accessible, high-quality structured data for reliable downstream artificial intelligence applications.

documents.abstract: Hourly reference evapotranspiration (ET0) forecasting plays a critical role in irrigation scheduling, water resource planning, and climate-resilient agricultural management. Short-term multi-horizon forecasting of hourly ET0 remains relatively underexplored, particularly using automated forecasting frameworks and emerging time-series foundation models. This study proposes an automated multi-horizon forecasting framework for hourly ET0 prediction using statistical, tabular, ensemble, deep-learning, and foundation forecasting paradigms implemented through the AutoGluon TimeSeries (AG-TS) framework. Hourly ET₀ values were computed using the ASCE Penman–Monteith equation from meteorological observations collected between October 2015 and December 2025. Forecasting experiments were conducted for four operational horizons (1-h, 6-h, 24-h, and 168-h) using SeasonalNaive, Theta, ETS, RecursiveTabular, DirectTabular, WeightedEnsemble, Temporal Fusion Transformer (TFT), and Chronos2 models. Results revealed horizon-dependent model behaviour, with Chronos2 achieving superior performance at the 1-h and 168-h forecasting horizons, while WeightedEnsemble demonstrated better predictive capability at the 6-h and 24-h horizons. Comparative analysis further indicated that Chronos2 maintained competitive forecasting accuracy with comparatively moderate computational demand, whereas TFT incurred substantially higher training costs despite rapid inference capability. These findings demonstrate the potential of automated forecasting frameworks for robust multi-horizon ET0 prediction and highlight the emerging applicability of pretrained time-series foundation models for operational hydrological and agro-environmental forecasting tasks.

Autonomous vehicles are an emerging technology that combines Artificial Intelligence (AI), cloud computing, sensors, and communication networks to support intelligent transportation. Cloud systems play an important role in data storage, processing, monitoring, and software updates. However, the increasing connectivity of autonomous vehicles also introduces several cybersecurity risks.This research presents a review of security threats and challenges associated with autonomous vehicles and cloud systems. It examines threats such as sensor spoofing, denial-of service attacks, vehicle network manipulation, AI-based attacks, cloud vulnerabilities, and communication security issues. The study also reviews risk assessment techniques, including STRIDE, DREAD, and CVSS, along with security measures such as encryption, authentication, intrusion detection, and secure software updates. The review highlights the importance of protecting vehicle systems, communication networks, and cloud infrastructure through a layered security approach. It also identifies areas requiring further research to improve the safety, reliability, and cybersecurity of autonomous transportation.

Artificial intelligence (AI) and laboratory automation now operate inside the core loop of physics research. They design optical experiments, shape fusion plasmas, decode quantum errors, select particle collisions in real time and propose new crystals. Existing reviews catalogue these applications by subfield, yet none measures how much decision authority each system holds or how rigorously its outputs are checked. This study introduces two ordinal scales, the Physics Research Autonomy Levels (PRAL, L0 to L5) and the Verification Levels (VL, V0 to V5), and applies them to sixteen documented systems published between 2016 and 2025 in quantum, plasma, particle, gravitational, condensed matter, materials and atmospheric physics. Each system is coded across six research stages: hypothesis, design, execution, analysis, interpretation and reporting. Three results follow. First, autonomy has advanced furthest in execution, where five physics systems act without per-decision human approval, while hypothesis selection and interpretation remain largely human. Second, reported gains concentrate on closed tasks with a fixed objective and a checkable answer, with accelerations from 16 to 2 billion times and equation recovery of 100%, whereas the strongest language model solves 5.7% of open research-level physics challenges. Third, autonomy and verification show no significant association across the corpus (Spearman rho = 0.14, p = 0.59). All four systems whose autonomy exceeds their verification by two or more levels act in hypothesis, design or interpretation, while no system confined to execution or analysis shows such a deficit. This difference is defined here as the verification gap. A Verification-Proportional Reporting checklist is proposed that scales evidence requirements with autonomy. The analysis indicates that the binding constraint on AI-driven physics has shifted from computational capability to verification capacity.

documents.abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.

Organizations undergoing large-scale agile transformations are increasingly introducing generative AI (GenAI) tools into everyday work. While GenAI promises to accelerate software development, less is known about how organizations integrate GenAI into existing large-scale agile ways of working and how it interacts with tensions related to autonomy, alignment, learning, and coordination. We examine barriers to GenAI integration through an exploratory case study of a large Nordic media organization undergoing a large-scale agile transformation. The findings reveal team-level barriers, including diverging AI beliefs, lack of shared practices, and limited experimentation capacity, and organizational-level barriers, including uneven AI maturity, weak organizational learning mechanisms, and cross-unit coordination and alignment challenges. Our findings suggest that GenAI does not create new organizational challenges but becomes intertwined with existing tensions in large-scale agile transformation and may intensify challenges related to learning, coordination, governance, and trust. We contribute to large-scale agile transformation research by showing how GenAI interacts with ongoing organizational change and by identifying conditions for sustainable GenAI integration at scale.

documents.abstract: Digital technologies, including analytics, algorithmic monitoring and generative artificial intelligence (AI), shape how organisations manage creative work, yet their implications for workplace sustainability remain insufficiently integrated in the existing literature. This perspective develops a process-based creativity management framework through a purposive synthesis of research on creativity, information systems, AI and workplace sustainability. An affordance perspective identifies actor-dependent possibilities for action, while a paradox perspective interprets tensions between augmentation and constraint that may recur across projects. The framework links four managerial functions (planning, organising, motivating and controlling) to digital affordances, tensions and proposed managerial conditions, with generative AI treated as a cross-cutting technology. It distinguishes gains in managerial information from employees’ autonomy, intrinsic motivation and willingness to share tentative ideas, while recognising constraints arising from the organisation of joint ideation. Six testable propositions specify actors and mechanisms at individual and team levels; the sixth links functions across project cycles. The theoretical contribution is to show how function-specific tensions may compound across project cycles and affect the psychological conditions that sustain creative work. Practically, the framework identifies configuration choices for feedback, monitoring, analytics and AI-assisted ideation, distinguishing short-term output gains from the long-term capacity of employees and teams to sustain creativity and well-being.

The opposition of scientific fact and religious faith is a familiar starting point for modern debates about knowledge, but it does not adequately describe either scientific practice or religious life. Science depends on observation, measurement, modelling and critical testing, yet its claims are also theory-laden, probabilistic and reversible. Religious traditions make claims through revelation, trust, interpretation, testimony and lived transformation; these claims cannot simply be translated into laboratory hypotheses. That is to say that, human knowing is often presented through a binary epistemological model in which science is associated with fact, evidence and empirical verification, while religion is associated with faith, revelation and transcendence. Although this distinction is useful, it becomes inadequate when treated as an absolute division between what can be known and what can only be believed. Contemporary developments in science, particularly quantum physics, cosmology, artificial intelligence and the study of consciousness, increasingly reveal the significance of probability, uncertainty, theoretical possibility and interpretative structures within scientific inquiry itself. Similarly, religious faith cannot be reduced to irrational or evidentially empty belief, since it incorporates reason, experience, tradition, interpretation and existential commitment. This paper, therefore, moves beyond the conventional fact–faith dichotomy and proposes an Afromodal philosophy of knowing grounded in the recognition of multiple but interconnected modes of human knowing. Drawing from Afromodalism, the paper argues that knowledge is not exhausted by empirical fact nor confined to religious faith; rather, human knowing emerges through an interplay of evidence, reason, experience, possibility, probability, intuition and meaning. The Afromodal perspective consequently seeks neither to subordinate science to religion nor religion to science, but to situate both within a broader epistemic horizon in which different modes of knowing can encounter one another without losing their distinctive identities. The paper concludes that moving beyond fact and faith is not a movement away from truth, but an invitation to rethink the plurality, relationality and situatedness of human knowing.

Organizations now have access to unprecedented compute, generative AI tools, multi-agent workflows, and data analytics capabilities, yet most AI initiatives fail to produce measurable transformation. This paper draws on sixteen transcribed sessions of the Barton College Data Analytics Consortium (October 2025–June 2026), a group of educators and practitioners in higher education, data science consulting, and industrial engineering, read alongside change-management, behavioral, and AI-productivity literature. We argue that the primary bottleneck to AI-driven transformation is neither financial nor technical but organizational: the human behavior that resists change. We identify eight distinct sources of resistance grouped into three families (threat-based, principled, and experiential), describe a “fluency trap” in which polished AI output suppresses scrutiny, and show that data literacy is a frequently missing prerequisite for AI readiness. Case evidence contrasts the automation of existing tasks with genuine agentic redesign of work. We conclude with a three-step framework for adoption (fix the process first, commit to scaling rather than downsizing, and run low-stakes, high-visibility pilots) and argue that without confronting behavioral inertia, organizations do not innovate; they simply produce, in one author’s words, “a digital version of a crappy process.”
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Manual scavenging remains a major test of the Indian state’s capacity to translate legal prohibition into substantive social change. This paper examines how the performance of government programmes should be assessed when a nationwide survey reports no identified manual scavengers, while hazardous sanitation work and related fatalities continue to raise public concern. The study adopts qualitative documentary analysis, drawing on government statements, statutory provisions, judicial decisions, and published research. It distinguishes manual scavenging as defined by law from hazardous cleaning of sewers and septic tanks, because the two categories are related but are not legally interchangeable. The analysis finds that official identification figures, rehabilitation assistance, training data, and recorded FIRs are important indicators of administrative activity; however, these outputs do not by themselves establish eradication, successful enforcement, or lasting occupational mobility. It further argues that death statistics must be interpreted in light of classification practices, reporting coverage, and the availability of case-level information. The paper also highlights a less visible dimension of the problem: occupational illness and delayed health consequences may remain difficult to connect to sanitation work in the absence of exposure histories and systematic occupational-health surveillance. These issues are inseparable from caste-based occupational marginalisation, which has historically restricted the livelihood choices of affected communities. The paper proposes an evidence-based framework for evaluating state performance through the completeness of identification, prevention, enforcement outcomes, rehabilitation results, occupational-health monitoring, and community participation. It concludes that claims of eradication require transparent methods, independent verification, and evidence that affected workers have secured safe and sustainable alternatives. The central measure of state success must therefore be the lived outcome for workers, rather than administrative declarations alone
