documents.abstract: The continuous evolution of societal dynamics profoundly shapes how individuals perceive, evaluate, and comply with the law. Within this context, legal philosophy plays a pivotal role in cultivating legal consciousness, as law cannot be reduced merely to a set of formal rules; rather, it constitutes a value-laden system anchored in justice, legal certainty, and utility. This study examines the role of legal philosophy in fostering public legal consciousness and identifies the structural and sociocultural challenges impeding that process. Employing a normative juridical methodology with philosophical and conceptual approaches, this research conducts a qualitative literature review of foundational theories, doctrines, and contemporary socio-legal scholarship. The findings demonstrate that legal philosophy nurtures critical and reflective reasoning regarding the nature, purpose, and normative foundations of law. Legal consciousness extends beyond mere knowledge of statutory provisions to encompass comprehension, evaluative attitudes, institutional trust, and an internalized willingness to adopt law as a guide for social conduct. Nevertheless, cultivating such consciousness faces persistent obstacles, including low legal literacy, tensions between positive law and community moral norms, eroding public trust in legal institutions, the rapid spread of misinformation via digital technology and artificial intelligence, and widespread civic apathy toward legal compliance. Consequently, legal philosophy occupies a strategic position in fostering a critical, rational, and value-oriented legal consciousness capable of sustaining compliance, justice, social order, and legal protection.

When a vulnerability at a security boundary of an LLM agent framework is patched, the advisory identifies the affected and patched versions, and replaying the proof-of-concept (PoC) tests only whether its reported trigger is still reproducible. That the trigger no longer fires does not, on its own, show that the underlying security invariant holds on every code path that reaches the boundary. We present a small, control-gated reconstruction method and a pilot study built around one question: can original-trigger replay report a boundary as fixed while the same invariant stays violable through a distinct, separately reachable path at the same version? We compare original trigger replay (B0) with a distinct sibling-path probe (M) for PraisonAI, and perform five additional before/after reconstructions across Langroid, Agno, and CrewAI. Each run emits a tri-state verdict of VIOLATION, NO_VIOLATION_OBSERVED, or INCONCLUSIVE. A mandatory pos itive (authorized) control gates the verdict, so that a non-violation result is admitted only when the control passes in the same run. All probes are benign, using an in-memory flag, a filesystem sentinel, or a builtins reachability check, and none performs a real payload. Our central result reproduces an officially recognized incomplete fix. In PraisonAI, original trigger replay reports the tool-loading boundary as fixed at version 4.6.31, yet the invariant is still violated through the tool_override path. That residual was later assigned its own identifier (CVE-2026-44334, catalogued as a “CVE-2026-40287 patch bypass”) and closed at 4.6.32. The five before/after measurements span four frameworks and four invariant classes. For a CVE whose advisory records no fixed version, we observe confinement in tested release 1.11.1 after observing a violation in 1.11.0. We are explicit about scope. A non-violation verdict means “no violation observed under the tested probe, version, and configuration,” not a proof of safety. The headline harness is control-gated per path, and fourteen fault-injection scenarios produced their expected verdicts. Only one same-version B0̸=M divergence is demonstrated. The PraisonAI probe invokes the documented loader functions directly, which establishes boundary behavior under the supplied setup rather than a full end-to-end exploit. Finally, we do not claim the method is a new testing technique or that it estimates prevalence.

Generative AI (Gen AI) has exposed and intensified a long-standing gap between academic products, such as papers and presentations, and the learning processes those products are often assumed to represent. The gap between process and product was always there, and had been widening for a while. This article examines how several pre-AI frameworks no longer adequately account for this shift. We first review earlier efforts to expand Bloom’s cognitive focus, including the models of Marzano and Kendall and L. Dee Fink. We then examine post-AI frameworks such as Michelle Kassorla’s Inverted Bloom’s Taxonomy and Tina Austin’s UnBlooms™ framework. Together, these frameworks suggest that GenAI exposes fundamental weaknesses in existing assessment structures and necessitates a rethinking of how evidence of learning is defined in AI-mediated contexts. How should learning taxonomies and assessment frameworks be reconfigured when GenAI weakens the traditional assumption that academic products reliably demonstrate student learning? Through a conceptual/theoretical analysis of pre-AI and post-AI learning frameworks, we examine how Bloom’s Taxonomy, Marzano and Kendall’s New Taxonomy, Fink’s Significant Learning, Inverted Bloom’s, and UnBlooms™ account for process, product, agency, and metacognition in Higher Education.

documents.abstract: Domain specialization of LLM agents is usually framed as a weight-update problem: collect trajectories, run reinforcement learning (RL) or supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and deploy a new checkpoint. We study a complementary axis: evolving the \textbf{agent harness}---the system prompt, tool schemas, skill library, and planning scaffolding---while keeping the policy frozen. We cast harness evolution as an RL-style outer loop and instantiate it with GEPA, a reflective evolutionary optimizer. The resulting harness adapters require no GPU training, are loadable per vertical domain, and compose with weight-based RL. Experiments with Codev, a Claude Code-style coding agent, on SWE-bench Verified, OfficeBench, and Terminal-Bench show a consistent pattern: weight updates give the strongest single-path gains, harness evolution recovers most of those gains at a small fraction of the compute, and combining both paths is best overall. We also analyze a failure mode of SFT-based specialization---shortened reasoning chains and increased truncation---and argue that harness adapters avoid it by construction. Our results position harness evolution as a practical, non-destructive complement to weight updates for vertical agents.

As critical fastening components in the member systems of transmission towers, bolted connections directly affect the safe and reliable operation of the entire system once loosening occurs. Traditional manual inspection methods are inefficient and highly subjective, making them unable to meet the need for continuous and online monitoring in modern engineering. In recent years, intelligent bolt loosening detection techniques based on multi-physical signals, such as acoustic and mechanical signals, have received considerable attention in the field of structural health monitoring (SHM), owing to their advantages of rapidity, efficiency, and online deployment capability. This paper systematically reviews existing techniques for bolt loosening detection, with particular emphasis on vibration analysis and guided wave-based methods. By integrating artificial intelligence, this paper further discusses the prospects of machine learning-driven bolt loosening state sensing and intelligent diagnosis methods. Finally, this paper analyzes the challenges to bolt loosening detection for ultra-high-voltage (UHV) transmission towers subjected to extreme service conditions, including environmental interference and degradation of monitoring performance. This work aims to provide a reference for the development and engineering application of SHM technologies for bolted connection structures.

The rapid integration of artificial intelligence into digital commerce has fundamentally disrupted the foundational doctrines of trademark law and transformed the relationship between consumers and commercial brands. For over a century, trademark jurisprudence in both common law and civil law traditions has rested on a foundational behavioral assumption: the "reasonably prudent consumer," an anthropomorphic standard possessing imperfect recollection, selective attention, and human cognitive vulnerabilities. This consumer navigated physical aisles and digital search results, using trademarks as informational heuristics to minimize search costs, identify commercial origin, and guarantee product quality. In the emerging artificial intelligence economy—governed by autonomous purchasing agents, large language model shopping assistants, predictive replenishment Internet-of-Things ecosystems, and opaque algorithmic recommendation engines—this cognitive interface is being systematically dismantled. Purchasing decisions are increasingly delegated to machine agents that evaluate multi-parameter multidimensional data vectors rather than perceiving visual brand iconography or sensory trade dress. Consequently, trademarks are being relegated from external communicative signifiers to latent data tokens embedded within neural network model weights and proprietary platform ranking architectures. This paper undertakes a comprehensive doctrinal, technological, and comparative examination of the profound legal, regulatory, and enforcement crises emerging at this junction of trademarks, technology, and commercial trust. First, it surveys the applicable statutory frameworks across major jurisdictions, including the United States Lanham Act, the European Union Trade Mark Regulation and Digital Services Act, the United Kingdom Trade Marks Act 1994, and the Indian Trade Marks Act, 1999 and Information Technology Act, 2000. Second, it synthesizes seminal and emerging judicial jurisprudence, tracing the doctrinal progression from early keyword advertising disputes—such as Google France, Rescuecom, and Interflora—to contemporary algorithmic marketplace gatekeeping conflicts exemplified by Multi Time Machine v. Amazon, Lush v. Amazon, Coty Germany, Christian Louboutin v. Nakul Bajaj, and the landmark CJEU Christian Louboutin v. Amazon decisions. Third, the study identifies critical legal and institutional gaps, demonstrating how modern machine-mediated commerce eviscerates conventional notions of "trademark use in commerce," renders initial interest and post-sale confusion doctrines conceptually incongruous, and immunizes dominant e-commerce intermediaries through outdated notice-and-takedown safe harbors. Fourth, it analyzes the severe enforcement and accountability challenges arising from non-deterministic algorithmic black boxes, where dynamic brand steering, private-label cannibalization, and synthetic trademark dilution occur without actionable human intent or transparent algorithmic accountability. Finally, evaluating international developments and emerging governance frameworks—such as the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act and Digital Markets Act alongside ongoing World Intellectual Property Organization initiatives—the paper proposes a multidimensional normative framework. It recommends the statutory codification of "algorithmic trademark use," the judicial adoption of a "dual-audience" confusion test separating human from autonomous synthetic purchasers, mandatory algorithmic brand neutrality and transparency audit obligations for dominant digital gatekeepers, and technical verification protocols for brand authentication within autonomous agent ecosystems. By recalibrating intellectual property frameworks to account for autonomous machine agency, this paper seeks to preserve the essential functions of trademarks: safeguarding market transparency, incentivizing quality investment, and sustaining consumer trust in an algorithmic economy.

Industrial Internet-of-Things environments generate heterogeneous sensor streams, topology metadata, and operational logs that must support forecasting, anomaly detection, and operator-facing explanation under deployment constraints. We present BRIDGE (Big data-driven Real-time Industrial multi-modal Decision support via Graph-Enhanced modeling), a topology- and log-aware industrial time-series framework that integrates: (i) a Graph-enhanced Topology Encoder using physical, metadata-based, training-only inferred, or identity graphs; (ii) an xLSTM temporal backbone trained with Contiguous Graph Patch Masking to simulate localized sensor outages; and (iii) an optional Cross-modal LLM Alignment module that generates reports without fine-tuning the LLM backbone. Because no single benchmark contains all modalities, we distinguish numerical-only, topology-aware, and log-enhanced evidence tiers. BRIDGE is evaluated on GiftEval-ZS and Chronos-ZS forecasting benchmarks, four industrial anomaly benchmarks, and 200 log-enhanced report windows. It obtains a CRPS of 0.396 on GiftEval-ZS and an $$F_1$$ score of $$92.4\%$$ on SMAP. The numerical predictive path requires 12 ms per sample at batch size 128 on the tested hardware, excluding autoregressive LLM decoding. The results support topology-aware integration for industrial monitoring while limiting claims about complete multi-modal effectiveness to the modalities actually evaluated.

Japanese historical documents, encompassing formats such as mokkan , kuzushiji manuscripts, and kindai records, represent a continuous documentary heritage linking the Nara period to the modern era. However, the scripts, layouts, and preservation states of these materials pose unique challenges for accessibility, particularly given the scarcity of specialists capable of reading cursive historical scripts such as kuzushiji. This survey provides a comprehensive examination of the recognition and analysis of Japanese historical documents, integrating perspectives from linguistic history, paleography, and computer vision. We review the evolution of the Japanese writing system, outline key challenges in historical document analysis, and present detailed case studies on recognition technologies for mokkan, kuzushiji, and kindai sources. Advances in deep learning, particularly in convolutional and transformer-based models, have improved transcription accuracy and enabled applications in digital humanities, education, archival search, and historical linguistics. We further explore recent trends in pretrained vision–language models, large language model integration, few-shot and zero-shot learning, multimodal reasoning, and self-supervised approaches. Finally, we identify open problems including cross-collection generalization, rare character recognition, interactive tools for humanities scholars, and deeper Natural Language Processing integration, and emphasize the need for sustained collaboration between machine learning and humanities to preserve and revitalize Japan’s written heritage as an accessible resource for global research.

Characterising individual cells is fundamental to computational pathology, as cellular morphology informs tasks such as tumour grading, mitotic assessment and immune profiling. However, most pathology foundation models are trained on tissue patches and capture cellular features only implicitly, while existing cell-level models are either restricted to specific cell populations or rely on computationally expensive architectures with hundreds of millions of parameters. Applying ViTs directly to small cellular crops also presents an architectural challenge: upsampling increases computational cost without adding morphological information and may introduce interpolation artefacts. To address these limitations, we introduce C-LiTE, a lightweight foundation model for cellular representation learning in H&E-stained histopathology, with only 22 million parameters. C-LiTE employs a native-resolution tokenisation strategy tailored to cellular inputs, processing 64 x 64 px cell-centred crops using a 4 x 4 patch embedding to produce a 16 x 16 token grid without image upsampling. To transfer visual knowledge from large-scale pre-training, we adapt the patch embedding weights of a pre-trained ViT-5-S using a pseudoinverse-based transformation, enabling weight initialisation at the finer patch resolution. We further assemble a pre-training dataset of 60 million cell-centred crops from TCGA, balanced across 19 cancer types and 16 tissue types. To our knowledge, this represents the largest public dataset for self-supervised pre-training on H&E images at the cellular level. We evaluate C-LiTE on seven public datasets spanning mitotic figure recognition, nucleus and cell-type classification, and immune cell phenotyping. Under frozen-feature evaluation, C-LiTE achieves a mean macro-F1 of 0.670, approaching CytoFormer (0.682) with approximately 30x fewer parameters.
